Let $f:X\\to[0,+\\infty]$ be measurable and define\n$$\\nu_f(A):=\\int_A f\\,d\\mu \\qquad (A\\in\\mathcal A).$$\nThen $\\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\\mathcal A)$.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** An arbitrary measure space $(X,\\mathcal A,\\mu)$; a nonnegative measurable function $f$.\n\n[L1] The set function $A\\mapsto\\int_A f\\,d\\mu$ is defined by $A\\mapsto\\int f\\chi_A\\,d\\mu$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).\n\n[L2] Monotone convergence holds for the nonnegative integral ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).\n\n[L3] The nonnegative integral is additive on measurable sets ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).\n\n[L4] A measure must vanish at the empty set and be countably additive on disjoint measurable sequences ([[def-measure]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 One has $\\nu_f(\\varnothing)=0$. If $(A_n)$ is a pairwise disjoint sequence, put $B_n:=\\bigcup_{k<n}A_k$. Then $\\chi_{B_n}\\uparrow\\chi_{\\bigcup_kA_k}$, so $f\\chi_{B_n}\\uparrow f\\chi_{\\bigcup_kA_k}$, including where $f=+\\infty$ under the convention $0\\cdot\\infty=0$. By [L2], $\\nu_f(\\bigcup_kA_k)=\\lim_n\\nu_f(B_n)$. [L1, L2, given]\n\n2.1 Because the sets $A_k$ are disjoint, $f\\chi_{B_n}=\\sum_{k<n}f\\chi_{A_k}$. Repeated use of [L3] gives $\\nu_f(B_n)=\\sum_{k<n}\\nu_f(A_k)$. Taking the increasing limit in step 1.1 proves countable additivity. [step 1.1, L3, algebra]\n\n3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verify the two conditions in [L4], so $\\nu_f$ is a measure. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4] ∎ ",

Hunter, Measure Theory Notes, Proposition 4.5\"\n      url: \"https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch4.pdf\"\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $(X,\\mathcal A,\\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\\to[0,+\\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\\ge0$.\n\n1. If $f\\le g$, then $\\int f\\,d\\mu\\le\\int g\\,d\\mu$.\n2. If $c>0$, then $\\int cf\\,d\\mu=c\\int f\\,d\\mu$. For $c=0$,\n   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the\n   undefined extended-real product $0\\cdot(+\\infty)$.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** An arbitrary measure space $(X,\\mathcal A,\\mu)$; nonnegative measurable functions $f,g$ and a scalar $c\\ge0$.\n\n[L1] The nonnegative integral is the supremum of simple minorants ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).\n\n[L2] On simple functions, the nonnegative and simple integrals agree ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).\n\n[L3] The simple integral is homogeneous for positive scalars and has zero integral on the zero simple function ([[prop-basic-properties-of-the-nonnegative-simple-integral]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 If $f\\le g$, every simple minorant of $f$ is also a simple minorant of $g$. Taking suprema in [L1] gives $\\int f\\,d\\mu\\le\\int g\\,d\\mu$. [L1, given]\n\n1.2 The zero function has just one nonnegative simple minorant: itself. [L1, L2, L3] Its simple integral is $0$ by [L3], so [L1] gives integral $0$ for the zero function, even on a space of infinite measure. [L1, L2, L3]\n\n2.1 For $c>0$, multiplication by $c$ bijects simple minorants of $f$ with those of $cf$. The inverse divides by $c$ and preserves nonnegativity and simplicity. By [L2] and [L3], the corresponding simple integrals differ by the factor $c$. Multiplication by a positive finite real commutes with the supremum in $[0,+\\infty]$, including when that supremum is infinite. Hence $\\int cf\\,d\\mu=c\\int f\\,d\\mu$. Together with steps 1.1 and 1.2, this proves both clauses. [L1, given, algebra, L2, L3] ∎\n\n",

Hunter, Measure Theory Notes, Definition 4.4\"\n      url: \"https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch4.pdf\"\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nIf $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative\nLebesgue integral equals its simple integral:\n$$\\int s\\,d\\mu=\\int_{\\mathrm{simple}} s\\,d\\mu.$$\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** A nonnegative simple measurable function $s$.\n\n[L1] The nonnegative integral is the supremum of the simple integrals of all simple minorants $0\\le u\\le s$ ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).\n\n[L2] The simple integral is monotone on nonnegative simple functions ([[prop-basic-properties-of-the-nonnegative-simple-integral]]).\n\n[L3] The simple integral itself is well defined on every nonnegative simple function ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 The function $s$ is one of its own admissible simple minorants, so [L1] gives $$\\int s\\,d\\mu\\ge\\int_{\\mathrm{simple}} s\\,d\\mu.$$ [given, L1, L3]\n\n1.2 If $u$ is any admissible simple minorant of $s$, then $u\\le s$, so [L2] gives $$\\int_{\\mathrm{simple}} u\\,d\\mu\\le\\int_{\\mathrm{simple}} s\\,d\\mu.$$ Taking the supremum over all such $u$ in [L1] yields the reverse inequality. [L1, L2, L3]\n\n2.1 The two inequalities from steps 1.1 and 1.2 give equality of the nonnegative and simple integrals on $s$. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎ ",

Hunter, Measure Theory (UC Davis lecture notes), Proposition 2.7\"\n      url: \"https://metaphor.ethz.ch/x/2022/fs/401-4820-22L/notes/Mean-Field_Limits_in_Statistical_Dynamics_Golse.pdf\"\n    - title: \"T. Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory (GSM 126), Section 1.2\"\n      url: \"https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf\"\npipeline_run: null\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $n \\ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**\n([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \\le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write\n\n$$R^{\\circ} := \\{\\, x \\in \\mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \\text{ for every } i<n \\,\\}, \\qquad \\overline{R} := [a,b] = \\{\\, x \\in \\mathbb{R}^n : a_i \\le x_i \\le b_i \\text{ for every } i<n \\,\\}$$\n\n([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\\circ}$ is open and\n$\\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**\nset $R$ with $R^{\\circ} \\subseteq R \\subseteq \\overline{R}$ is Lebesgue\nmeasurable with\n\n$$\\lambda_n(R) \\;=\\; \\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$\n\nIn particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each\ncoordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box\n$B(a,b) = \\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of\nthem, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them\nwhenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite\nparameters the value is already\n$\\lambda_n(B) = \\operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** A natural number $n \\ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, reals $a_i \\le b_i$ for $i<n$, and the sets $R^\\circ$, $\\overline{R}$ displayed in the Statement.\n\n[L1] Assuming countable choice, $\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra, $\\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it, every set of Lebesgue outer measure zero is Lebesgue measurable of measure zero, and $\\lambda_n(B) = \\operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).\n\n[L2] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).\n\n[L3] Assuming countable choice, $\\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]), so it is monotone and countably subadditive ([[def-outer-measure]], [[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]).\n\n[L4] For a nonempty box $\\operatorname{vol}(B) := \\prod_{i<n}(b_i - a_i)$ when every $a_i$ and every $b_i$ is real, and a box is nonempty exactly when $a_i < b_i$ for every $i < n$ ([[def-half-open-box]]).\n\n[F1] $[a,b]:=\\{x\\in\\mathbb R^m:a_j\\le x_j\\le b_j\\ (j<m)\\}$ and $\\operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).\n\n[F2] A **measure** on $(X,\\mathcal A)$ is a function $\\mu:\\mathcal A\\to[0,+\\infty]$ with $\\mu(\\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive on pairwise disjoint sequences ([[def-measure]]).\n\n[F3] For every real $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $k \\ge 1$ with $1/k < \\varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).\n\n[F4] $\\prod_{k<n}(a_kb_k) = (\\prod_{k<n}a_k)(\\prod_{k<n}b_k)$; if $a_k \\ge 0$ for all $k<n$ then $\\prod_{k<n} a_k \\ge 0$, with $\\prod_{k<n}a_k>0$ when every $a_k>0$; and finite products are defined by the recursion $\\Pi_0 = 1$, $\\Pi_{\\sigma(n)} = \\Pi_n \\cdot a_n$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claim 6; [[def-finite-sum]]).\n\n[F5] A subset $U \\subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \\in U$ there is a real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \\subseteq U$; a subset $F$ is **closed** if its complement is open ([[def-metric-topology]]).\n\n[F6] The forms $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are **half-open**, and an interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, **closed** when both are included ([[def-interval]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 $R^{\\circ}$ is open and $\\overline{R}$ is closed in $(\\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$, by the same coordinatewise estimate in each case, so both are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. [L2, F1, F5, F6]\n\n1.2 A closed rectangle with a degenerate side is Lebesgue null: let $u_i \\le v_i$ be reals with $u_{i_0} = v_{i_0} = c$ for some $i_0 < n$, and let $\\eta$ be a positive real; the half-open box with parameter pairs $(u_i-1, v_i]$ for $i \\ne i_0$ and $(c-\\eta, c]$ in coordinate $i_0$ is nonempty, contains $[u,v]$, and has volume $\\eta\\,C$ where $C := \\prod_{i<n}w_i > 0$ with $w_{i_0} := 1$ and $w_i := v_i-u_i+1$ otherwise, so monotonicity of the outer measure gives $\\lambda_n^*([u,v]) \\le \\eta C$ for every positive real $\\eta$ and hence $\\lambda_n^*([u,v]) = 0$. [L1, L3, L4, F1, F3, F4]\n\n2.1 The difference $\\overline{R} \\setminus R^{\\circ}$ is contained in the union of the $2n$ closed rectangles obtained from $[a,b]$ by replacing the $i$-th side by the degenerate side $[a_i,a_i]$ or by $[b_i,b_i]$, each of which is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, so countable subadditivity of the outer measure, applied to that finite list padded with empty sets, gives $\\lambda_n^*(\\overline{R}\\setminus R^{\\circ}) = 0$; every subset of $\\overline{R}\\setminus R^{\\circ}$ is therefore Lebesgue measurable of measure $0$. [step 1.2, L1, L3]\n\n2.2 Suppose instead $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for some $i_0<n$. Then $R^{\\circ} = \\varnothing$, the rectangle $\\overline{R}$ is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, every $R$ between them is a subset of it and so is measurable of measure $0$, and the product $\\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$ has the factor $0$ and is therefore $0$ as well. [step 1.2, L1, F4]\n\n3.1 Suppose first that $a_i < b_i$ for every $i<n$. Then $B(a,b)$ is a nonempty half-open box with $R^{\\circ} \\subseteq B(a,b) \\subseteq \\overline{R}$ and $\\lambda_n(B(a,b)) = \\operatorname{vol}(B(a,b)) = \\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$. For $R$ with $R^{\\circ}\\subseteq R\\subseteq\\overline{R}$, both $R \\setminus B(a,b)$ and $B(a,b)\\setminus R$ are contained in $\\overline{R}\\setminus R^{\\circ}$, hence are measurable of measure $0$ by step 2.1, so $R = \\big(B(a,b)\\setminus(B(a,b)\\setminus R)\\big)\\cup\\big(R\\setminus B(a,b)\\big)$ is measurable, and additivity on the two disjoint decompositions $R = (R\\cap B(a,b)) \\sqcup (R\\setminus B(a,b))$ and $B(a,b) = (R\\cap B(a,b)) \\sqcup (B(a,b)\\setminus R)$ gives $\\lambda_n(R) = \\lambda_n(R\\cap B(a,b)) = \\lambda_n(B(a,b))$. [step 2.1, L1, L4, F2]\n\n4.1 Steps 3.1 and 2.2 exhaust the two cases and give the displayed value in each, and step 1.1 supplies the Borel and measurability clauses for $R^{\\circ}$ and $\\overline{R}$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎\n",
    "items/lem-geometry-tensor-gap-bounds-cellwise-form-defect.md": "---\nid: lem-geometry-tensor-gap-bounds-cellwise-form-defect\nkind: lemma\ntitle: Cellwise geometry tensor gaps bound form error and stability loss\nstatus: draft\norigin: pipeline\npipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16\ndependency_level: 2\ndeps: [def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy, lem-discrete-form-perturbation-preserves-coercivity, def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms, thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions, thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives, thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals, thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm, def-countable-choice, thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure, thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one, thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]\nproof_strategy: direct\nprovenance:\n  statement: literature-derived\n  proof: ai-generated\nverification:\n  precheck: pending\nsources:\n  references:\n    - title: Jean-Luc Guermond, MATH 661 Fall 2025, Part VI, Chapter 27, Error analysis with variational crimes\n      url: https://people.tamu.edu/~guermond/M661_FALL_2025/chap27.pdf\n    - title: Joachim Schöberl, Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations, Chapter 25, Non-conforming Finite Element Methods\n      url: https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/FEM/nonconforming.html\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nAssume the geometry setting of [[def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy]], and suppose $\\Omega_h$ has a nonempty finite measurable partition into bounded cells $\\{K\\}$, with $h_K:=\\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and $h:=\\max_Kh_K$. For real-valued $U,W\\in C^1(\\Omega)$ with $\\nabla U,\\nabla W\\in L^2(\\Omega)$, put $v:=U\\circ\\Phi_h$ and $w:=W\\circ\\Phi_h$, and assume their gradients are square-integrable on each cell. Then the physical exact form $a(U,W)$ pulled back by $\\Phi_h$ is $a_h^{\\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)$. Suppose the implemented tensors $\\widetilde B_h$ are real symmetric and measurable, with $\\eta_{G,K}<\\infty$. The form $\\widetilde a_h(v,w):=\\sum_K\\int_K\\nabla v^T\\widetilde B_h\\nabla w$ satisfies\n\n$$|a_h^{\\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)-\\widetilde a_h(v,w)|\\le\\sum_K\\eta_{G,K}\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2(K)}\\|\\nabla w\\|_{L^2(K)}\\le\\eta_G\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2(\\Omega_h)}\\|\\nabla w\\|_{L^2(\\Omega_h)},$$\n\nwhere $\\eta_G:=\\max_K\\eta_{G,K}$. If $\\eta_{G,K}\\le C_Gh_K^s$ for $s>0$, the form defect is at most $C_Gh^s\\|\\nabla v\\|_2\\|\\nabla w\\|_2$. Moreover, if $J_h\\ge j_->0$, $0<L$, and $\\|D\\Phi_h\\|_{L^\\infty,\\mathrm{op}}\\le L$, then $B_h\\succeq\\beta I$ with $\\beta=j_-\\lambda/L^2$. For the stability conclusion, let $Z_h$ be a real Hilbert space of pullback functions with inner product $\\int_{\\Omega_h}\\nabla v\\cdot\\nabla w$, so its norm is $\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2(\\Omega_h)}$. Restrict the exact and implemented forms to $Z_h$. If $\\eta_G\\le\\beta/2$, the implemented form is coercive on $Z_h$ with constant at least $\\beta/2$. The rate assumption is separate from the lift; neither it nor completeness of the gradient-norm space follows from a lift alone.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** Countable Choice; the geometry definition; a nonempty finite measurable cell partition; physical functions $U,W$ and their pullbacks $v,w$ as stated; a real symmetric measurable tensor $A$ with $\\lambda I\\preceq A\\preceq\\Lambda I$; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with positive Jacobian; measurable symmetric implemented tensors $\\widetilde B_h$ with finite cell discrepancies; and, for the coercivity conclusion, the real Hilbert space $Z_h$ with the gradient inner product specified in the Statement.\n\n[F1] [[def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy]]: $B_h=J_hD\\Phi_h^{-1}(A\\circ\\Phi_h)D\\Phi_h^{-T}$ and $\\eta_{G,K}=\\|B_h-\\widetilde B_h\\|_{L^\\infty(K;\\mathrm{op})}$.\n\n[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: differentiating $U\\circ\\Phi_h$ gives $\\nabla(U\\circ\\Phi_h)=D\\Phi_h^T(\\nabla U\\circ\\Phi_h)$, so $\\nabla U\\circ\\Phi_h=D\\Phi_h^{-T}\\nabla(U\\circ\\Phi_h)$.\n\n[F3] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes variables by the positive factor $J_h$ for every nonnegative measurable integrand.\n\n[F4] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: integral Cauchy–Schwarz applies on each cell, and the finite sum of cell products is bounded by the product of the two Euclidean norms of the cellwise L2 norms.\n\n[F5] [[lem-discrete-form-perturbation-preserves-coercivity]]: a diagonal perturbation bounded by $\\eta\\|v\\|^2$ lowers a coercivity constant by at most $\\eta$.\n\n[F6] [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]: coercivity in a real Hilbert space means $a(v,v)\\ge\\alpha\\|v\\|^2$ for every vector.\n\n[F7] Nonnegative Lebesgue integration over measurable sets is a measure ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]), and the integral is linear on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). Finite products and sums of measurable real functions are measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).\n\n[A3] Countable Choice is the explicit assumption of the change-of-variables supplier [F3] ([[def-countable-choice]]).\n\n[A1] $J_h\\ge j_->0$, $0<L$, and $\\|D\\Phi_h\\|_{L^\\infty,\\mathrm{op}}\\le L$.\n\n[A2] On each cell $K$, $\\eta_{G,K}\\le C_Gh_K^s$ for the stated optional rate conclusion.\n\n## Proof\n\n1.1 Set $v=U\\circ\\Phi_h$ and $w=W\\circ\\Phi_h$. By [F2], $\\nabla U\\circ\\Phi_h=D\\Phi_h^{-T}\\nabla v$ and likewise for $W$. Under the Countable Choice hypothesis [A3], apply [F3] to the nonnegative measurable energy density $\\nabla U^TA\\nabla U$ to obtain $a(U,U)=a_h^{\\mathrm{lift}}(v,v)$; the same applies to $W$ and $U+W$. The physical energies are finite since $A\\preceq\\Lambda I$ and all three physical gradients are in $L^2$. Their nonnegative pulled-back energy densities therefore have finite integrals. The pointwise polarization identity expresses the pulled-back cross density as half the difference of these three integrable nonnegative densities, hence makes that cross density absolutely integrable. The physical cross density is integrable by the same argument. Since $A$ and $B_h$ are symmetric, the real polarization identity $2a(U,W)=a(U+W,U+W)-a(U,U)-a(W,W)$ yields $a(U,W)=a_h^{\\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)$. [F1, F2, F3, A3, given, algebra]\n\n1.2 For every vector $\\xi$, [A1] and $A\\succeq\\lambda I$ imply $\\xi^TB_h\\xi=J_h(D\\Phi_h^{-T}\\xi)^TA(\\Phi_h)(D\\Phi_h^{-T}\\xi)\\ge j_-\\lambda\\|D\\Phi_h^{-T}\\xi\\|^2\\ge(j_-\\lambda/L^2)\\|\\xi\\|^2$. Thus $B_h\\succeq\\beta I$. [F1, A1, given, algebra]\n\n2.1 The finite measurable partition and the assumed finite cellwise squared-gradient integrals give global square integrability: apply the measure property [F7] to $|\\nabla v|^2$ and $|\\nabla w|^2$ to obtain $\\|\\nabla v\\|_2^2=\\sum_K\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2(K)}^2$ and the analogous identity for $w$. The tensor and gradient entries are measurable, so the defect density $q=\\nabla v^T(B_h-\\widetilde B_h)\\nabla w$ is measurable by [F7]. On each cell $|q|\\le\\eta_{G,K}|\\nabla v||\\nabla w|$ almost everywhere; [F4] makes this an integrable majorant, and the finite sum makes $q$ globally $L^1$. Step 1.1 has established that the exact lifted cross density is $L^1$. Thus the implemented cross density, the exact cross density minus $q$, is also $L^1$. Their finite indicator decompositions over the partition and $L^1$ linearity [F7] justify subtracting and summing cell integrals. Hunter, Measure Theory Notes, Proposition 4.9\"\n      url: \"https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch4.pdf\"\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nThe class $L^1(\\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is\ncomplex-linear on it:\n$$\\int (\\alpha f+\\beta g)\\,d\\mu=\\alpha\\int f\\,d\\mu+\\beta\\int g\\,d\\mu \\qquad(\\alpha,\\beta\\in\\mathbb C,\\ f,g\\in L^1(\\mu)).$$\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** Integrable functions $f,g\\in L^1(\\mu)$ and scalars $\\alpha,\\beta\\in\\mathbb C$.\n\n[L1] Real and complex integrability, together with the decomposition into positive and negative parts and into real and imaginary parts, is defined in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].\n\n[L2] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).\n\n[L3] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).\n\n[L4] Sums and real scalar multiples of measurable real-valued functions are measurable ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 First treat real-valued $f,g$ and put $h:=f+g$. By [L4], the function $h$ is measurable. Also $$h^+\\le f^++g^+,\\qquad h^-\\le f^-+g^-,$$ so [L2] and [L3] give $$\\int h^+\\,d\\mu\\le\\int f^+\\,d\\mu+\\int g^+\\,d\\mu<+\\infty,\\qquad \\int h^-\\,d\\mu\\le\\int f^-\\,d\\mu+\\int g^-\\,d\\mu<+\\infty.$$ Hence $h$ is integrable. Since $$h^++f^-+g^-=h^-+f^++g^+,$$ another application of [L2] yields $$\\int h^+\\,d\\mu+\\int f^-\\,d\\mu+\\int g^-\\,d\\mu =\\int h^-\\,d\\mu+\\int f^+\\,d\\mu+\\int g^+\\,d\\mu,$$ which rearranges to $$\\int(f+g)\\,d\\mu=\\int f\\,d\\mu+\\int g\\,d\\mu.$$ [L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]\n\n1.2 Now let $c\\in\\mathbb R$ and let $f$ be real-valued. By [L4], $cf$ is measurable. If $c\\ge0$, then $$(cf)^+=cf^+,\\qquad (cf)^-=cf^-;$$ if $c<0$, then $$(cf)^+=(-c)f^-,\\qquad (cf)^-=(-c)f^+.$$ In both cases [L3] shows that $cf$ is integrable and that $$\\int(cf)\\,d\\mu=c\\int f\\,d\\mu.$$ [L1, L3, L4, algebra]\n\n2.1 Let $h=u+iv\\in L^1(\\mu)$ and $\\gamma=a+ib\\in\\mathbb C$. Then $$\\gamma h=(au-bv)+i(av+bu).$$ The real-valued functions $au-bv$ and $av+bu$ are integrable by steps 1.1 and 1.2, and their real-linear integral formulas combine into $$\\int(\\gamma h)\\,d\\mu=\\gamma\\int h\\,d\\mu.$$ Writing $\\alpha f=h_1+ik_1$ and $\\beta g=h_2+ik_2$ with real-valued integrable $h_j,k_j$, step 1.1 gives $$\\int(\\alpha f+\\beta g)\\,d\\mu =\\int(h_1+h_2)\\,d\\mu+i\\int(k_1+k_2)\\,d\\mu =\\int h_1\\,d\\mu+i\\int k_1\\,d\\mu+\\int h_2\\,d\\mu+i\\int k_2\\,d\\mu =\\alpha\\int f\\,d\\mu+\\beta\\int g\\,d\\mu.$$ [L1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎\n",
    "items/thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability.md": "---\nverification:\n  repair: research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-owner/published-repairs/thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability.json\nid: thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability\nkind: theorem\ntitle: \"Arithmetic and lattice operations preserve measurability whenever they are defined\"\nstatus: published\norigin: session\nprovenance:\n  statement: literature-derived\n  proof: ai-altered\ndeps: [def-extended-reals, def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function, def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product, thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability, lem-rat-embeds-dense, thm-rationals-countable, def-sigma-algebra, thm-sigma-algebra-closure-laws, def-complete-ordered-field]\nproof_strategy: direct\nsources:\n  references:\n    - title: \"Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration and Real Analysis, Section 2B\"\n      url: \"https://measure.axler.net/MIRA.pdf\"\n    - title: \"John K. Products of functions use\n$\\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$\nabbreviates $\\underline c\\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\\underline c$.\nThe magnitude function is $|f|=\\max(f,-f)$ as in\n[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:\n\n1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;\n2. $\\max(f,g)$, $\\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;\n3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;\n4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\\odot_X g$ is measurable.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\\mathcal A)$ and Borel-measurable functions $f,g:X\\to\\overline{\\mathbb R}$.\n\n[L1] Measurability is equivalent to measurability of all strict upper (or lower) real threshold sets. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])\n\n[L2] The parts are $h^+=\\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\\max(-h,0)$; $|h|=\\max(h,-h)$. At every point one part is zero. ([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]])\n\n[L3] Reflection reverses extended-real order. Partial addition excludes exactly the opposite-infinity pairs; addition with zero is defined. ([[def-extended-reals]])\n\n[L4] The total function product $u\\odot_X v$ is zero when either value is zero, is the real product on finite values, and otherwise is the infinity with the sign of the product. This includes all four ordered zero-infinity pairs. ([[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]])\n\n[L5] A sigma-algebra contains $X$ and the empty set and is closed under finite intersections and countable unions; the rationals are countable, and between distinct real numbers lies a rational. ([[def-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-sigma-algebra-closure-laws]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]])\n\n[L6] Finite real arithmetic is ordered-field arithmetic. ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 Scalar multiples are measurable. If $c>0$, the product clauses give $\\{cf>a\\}=\\{f>a/c\\}$ for every real $a$, including infinite values of $f$. If $c<0$, they give $\\{cf>a\\}=\\{f<a/c\\}$. If $c=0$, $cf$ is constantly zero, whose threshold sets are $X$ or empty. Thus [L1] proves the claim, including measurability of $-f$. The latter agrees pointwise with reflection by the finite and the two infinite sign cases. [given, L1, L3, L4, L5, L6]\n\n1.2 Assume $f+g$ is defined at every point. For every real $a$, $$\\{f+g>a\\}=\\bigcup_{q\\in\\mathbb Q}\\bigl(\\{f>q\\}\\cap\\{g>a-q\\}\\bigr).$$ To check the right-to-left inclusion, both values then exceed finite bounds, hence neither is $-\\infty$. If either is $+\\infty$, the sum is $+\\infty$; otherwise finite ordered-field addition gives $f(x)+g(x)>a$. Conversely, a defined sum greater than $a$ cannot have a $-\\infty$ summand. If both summands are finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<f(x)$. If $f(x)=+\\infty$ and $g(x)$ is finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<a-g(x)+1$. If $g(x)=+\\infty$ and $f(x)$ is finite, choose $f(x)-1<q<f(x)$. If both are $+\\infty$, take $q=0$. These are all cases. The union is countable and each intersection is measurable, proving measurability of the sum. [L1, L3, L5, L6]\n\n1.3 Let $u,v:X\\to[0,+\\infty]$ be measurable. Their product is nonnegative by [L4], so its strict upper threshold set is $X$ when $a<0$. For real $a\\ge0$, $$\\{u\\odot_X v>a\\}=\\bigcup_{q\\in\\mathbb Q,\\ q>0}\\bigl(\\{u>q\\}\\cap\\{v>a/q\\}\\bigr).$$ A point on the right has $u(x)>q>0$ and $v(x)>a/q\\ge0$. If either value is infinite the product is $+\\infty$; otherwise multiplying the strict finite bounds proves that the product exceeds $a$. Conversely, a product greater than $a\\ge0$ has neither value zero. If both values are finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<u(x)$, which is possible because $u(x)v(x)>a$. If $u(x)$ is finite positive and $v(x)=+\\infty$, choose $0<q<u(x)$. If $u(x)=+\\infty$ and $v(x)$ is finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<a/v(x)+1$; this ensures $q>0$, also at $a=0$. If both values are $+\\infty$, take $q=1$. These cases include $a=0$ and exclude zero-infinity pairs exactly because their product is zero. Countability and threshold measurability prove measurability of the nonnegative product. [L1, L4, L5, L6]\n\n2.1 For real $a$, total order gives $$\\{\\max(f,g)>a\\}=\\{f>a\\}\\cup\\{g>a\\},\\qquad \\{\\min(f,g)>a\\}=\\{f>a\\}\\cap\\{g>a\\}.$$ The threshold criterion gives measurability. The zero function is measurable, so this also gives measurability of $f^+$, $f^-$ and $|f|=\\max(f,-f)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L5]\n\n3.1 By step 2.1 the four parts $f^+,f^-,g^+,g^-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. Step 1.3 makes their four $\\odot_X$ products measurable. Define $$h_+=(f^+\\odot_X g^+)+(f^-\\odot_X g^-),\\qquad h_-=(f^+\\odot_X g^-)+(f^-\\odot_X g^+).$$ Each addition is defined because both summands are nonnegative, so step 1.2 proves that $h_+,h_-$ are measurable. If either original value is zero, all four products are zero. If both are positive, only $f^+\\odot_X g^+$ can be nonzero; if both are negative, only $f^-\\odot_X g^-$ can be nonzero. If $f(x)>0>g(x)$, only $f^+\\odot_X g^-$ can be nonzero; if $f(x)<0<g(x)$, only $f^-\\odot_X g^+$ can be nonzero. Thus at least one of $h_+(x),h_-(x)$ is zero in every case. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, L2, L3, L4]\n\n4.1 The sum $h_++(-h_-)$ is therefore defined at every point. It is measurable by steps 1.1 and 1.2. It equals $f\\odot_X g$: in the zero case both sides are zero; in the two same-sign cases step 3.1 leaves the nonnegative magnitude product in $h_+$ and zero in $h_-$, and in the two opposite-sign cases it leaves zero in $h_+$ and that magnitude product in $h_-$. When both original values are finite, the real sign rules identify the value with their real product. When at least one nonzero original value is infinite, the remaining magnitude product is $+\\infty$, and the reconstruction is respectively $+\\infty$ or $-\\infty$, exactly as [L4] requires. No extended-real distributivity or cancellation is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, L3, L4, L6]\n\n5.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove scalar and lattice closure, step 1.2 proves defined-sum closure, and step 4.1 proves product closure with the declared convention. These are all four assertions. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 4.1] ∎\n",
    "items/thm-second-strang-lemma-for-nonconforming-galerkin.md": "---\nid: thm-second-strang-lemma-for-nonconforming-galerkin\nkind: theorem\ntitle: Second Strang estimate with a bounded extension to the comparison space\nstatus: draft\norigin: pipeline\npipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16\ndependency_level: 1\ndeps: [def-variational-crime-error-framework, thm-lax-milgram, def-countable-choice]\nproof_strategy: direct\nprovenance:\n  statement: literature-derived\n  proof: ai-generated\nverification:\n  precheck: pending\nsources:\n  references:\n    - title: Jean-Luc Guermond, MATH 661 Fall 2025, Part VI, Chapter 27, Error analysis with variational crimes\n      url: https://people.tamu.edu/~guermond/M661_FALL_2025/chap27.pdf\n    - title: Joachim Schöberl, Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations, Chapter 25, Non-conforming Finite Element Methods\n      url: https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/FEM/nonconforming.html\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nAssume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\\times V\\to\\mathbb K$ bounded and coercive, and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\\|\\cdot\\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\\widetilde a_h:X_h\\times V_h\\to\\mathbb K$ is a bounded extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and\n\n$$\\|u-u_h\\|_h\\le(1+M_h/\\alpha_h)\\inf_{v_h\\in V_h}\\|u-v_h\\|_h+\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\\alpha_h,$$\n\nwhere $\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\\sup_{w_h\\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-\\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\\|w_h\\|_h$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.\n\nFor a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\\le\\overline M<\\infty$ and $\\alpha_h\\ge\\underline\\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\\inf_{v_h\\in V_h}\\|u-v_h\\|_h$, the uniform bound is\n$$\\|u-u_h\\|_h\\le(1+\\overline M/\\underline\\alpha)E_h+\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\\underline\\alpha.$$\nThus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** Countable Choice; the exact Hilbert problem on $V$; the nonconforming space $V_h$ and common comparison norm on $X_h$; a bounded extension $\\widetilde a_h$; discrete coercivity $\\alpha_h>0$; and a bounded discrete load.\n\n[F1] [[thm-lax-milgram]] under [[def-countable-choice]]: the exact bounded coercive Hilbert problem has a unique solution.\n\n[F2] By definition, $\\widetilde a_h$ agrees with $a_h$ on $V_h\\times V_h$ and $|\\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\\le M_h\\|z\\|_h\\|w_h\\|_h$ on $X_h\\times V_h$ ([[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]).\n\n[A1] $\\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)\\ge\\alpha_h\\|v_h\\|_h^2$ for every $v_h\\in V_h$.\n\n[A2] $\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ is the consistency residual at the exact solution, as defined in [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]].\n\n## Proof\n\n1.1 Apply [F1] on $V$ to obtain the unique exact solution $u$. [F1, given]\n\n1.2 The finite-dimensional Hilbert problem on $V_h$ has bounded coercive form $a_h$ and bounded load $F_h$, so the same Lax–Milgram theorem [F1] gives a unique $u_h\\in V_h$. [F1, A1, given]\n\n2.1 Fix $v_h\\in V_h$ and set $e_h:=u_h-v_h$. Then $e_h\\in V_h$, and [A1] gives $\\alpha_h\\|e_h\\|_h^2\\le\\operatorname{Re}a_h(e_h,e_h)=\\operatorname{Re}(F_h(e_h)-\\widetilde a_h(v_h,e_h))$. [A1, step 1.2, choose]\n\n3.1 By the discrete equation and extension identity, $a_h(e_h,e_h)=\\widetilde a_h(u-v_h,e_h)+F_h(e_h)-\\widetilde a_h(u,e_h)$. The extension bound [F2] and residual definition [A2] therefore give $\\alpha_h\\|e_h\\|_h^2\\le(M_h\\|u-v_h\\|_h+\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u))\\|e_h\\|_h$. [F2, A1, A2, step 2.1, algebra]\n\n4.1 If $e_h=0$ there is nothing to divide by; otherwise divide step 3.1 by $\\alpha_h\\|e_h\\|_h$. The triangle inequality gives $\\|u-u_h\\|_h\\le(1+M_h/\\alpha_h)\\|u-v_h\\|_h+\\delta_h^{\\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\\alpha_h$. Taking the infimum over $v_h$ proves the per-mesh bound. For the stated family, replace $M_h/\\alpha_h$ by $\\overline M/\\underline\\alpha$ and $1/\\alpha_h$ by $1/\\underline\\alpha$. The resulting constants are independent of $h$, yielding the stated uniform, convergence and rate consequences when the two explicit error terms have the corresponding control. [step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎\n",

No independent judge or whole-closure certification.\n    delegated_by: owner\nsources:\n  references:\n    - title: \"Gerald B. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.39\"\n      url: \"https://djvu.online/file/NPF4BEtSuqdFA\"\n    - title: \"John K. Hunter, Measure Theory, Theorem 5.21\"\n      url: \"https://metaphor.ethz.ch/x/2022/fs/401-4820-22L/notes/Mean-Field_Limits_in_Statistical_Dynamics_Golse.pdf\"\n---\n\n## Statement\n\nAssume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let\n$\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite\nmeasure spaces.\n\n1. If $f : X \\times Y \\to [0,\\infty]$ is $\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\\subseteq X$ and $B\\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\\overline{\\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x\\notin A$ and $f^y$ is $\\overline{\\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y\\notin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\\int_Y f_x\\,d\\overline\\nu$ for $x\\notin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\\int_X f^y\\,d\\overline\\mu$ for $y\\notin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and\n$$\\int f\\,d\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu}=\\int_X I_f\\,d\\mu=\\int_Y J_f\\,d\\nu.$$\n2. If $f \\in L^1(\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu})$, there are measurable null sets $A\\subseteq X$ and $B\\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.\n\n## Facts & Assumptions\n\n**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, two sigma-finite measure spaces, their completed product $\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu}$, and either a nonnegative $\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu}$-measurable function $f$ or an integrable function $f \\in L^1(\\overline{\\mu \\times \\nu})$.\n\n[L1] Assuming countable choice, a function measurable for a completion is almost everywhere equal to one measurable for the original sigma-algebra. ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]])\n\n[L2] Tonelli and Fubini hold on the uncompleted product sigma-algebra. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])\n\n[L3] Once both functions are integrable, the integral is unchanged by almost-everywhere equality. ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])\n\n[L4] On a complete measure space, almost-everywhere equality with a measurable function implies measurability. ([[thm-ae-equality-preserves-measurability-on-complete-spaces]])\n\n[L5] Integrable complex functions have integrable real and imaginary parts. ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]])\n\n[L6] The nonnegative integral is the supremum over nonnegative simple minorants ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]); simple integrals are computed by finite level-set sums, independently of representation ([[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]]). A completed measurable set is $E=A\\cup N$ with $A$ base measurable, $N$ contained in a base measurable null set, and $\\overline\\mu(E)=\\mu(A)$ ([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]). A nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it is zero almost everywhere ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).\n\n## Proof\n\n**Proof technique:** direct.\n\n1.1 We first justify two nonnegative transfer rules, allowing infinite integrals. On any measure space, if measurable $p,q\\ge0$ agree outside a measurable null set $Z$, take a nonnegative simple $s\\le p$ and replace each positive level set $E_j$ by $E_j\\setminus Z$, assigning zero on $Z$. The resulting simple $s_0$ is bounded by $q$ and has the same integral as $s$, since removing a measurable null set does not change a level-set measure. Zero coefficients contribute zero even on infinite-measure sets by [L6]. Taking suprema of simple minorants gives $\\int p\\le\\int q$; reversing them gives equality, without assuming finiteness. Also, for a base-measurable $p\\ge0$, its integral is unchanged on completion: every base simple minorant is a completed one, while for a completed simple minorant $s=\\sum_j c_j\\mathbf1_{E_j}\\le p$, [L6] supplies base sets $A_j\\subseteq E_j$ with $\\mu(A_j)=\\overline\\mu(E_j)$. Taking the disjoint level-set representation makes the $A_j$ disjoint. The base simple function $s_0=\\sum_j c_j\\mathbf1_{A_j}\\le s\\le p$ has the same integral; the two suprema are therefore equal. ## Statement

Let $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite interval partition, $h:=\max_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)$, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$. Let $I_hu$ be the continuous piecewise-linear function with nodal values $I_hu(x_j)=u(x_j)$. Then

$$\|(u-I_hu)'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

If $u(0)=u(1)=0$, then $I_hu$ also vanishes at both endpoints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite interval partition, $h$ its maximum cell length, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$.

[F1] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: if a differentiable function has an integrable derivative, its increment is the integral of that derivative.

[F2] [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]: for an integrable function bounded in absolute value by $C$, the integral over an interval of length $\ell$ has absolute value at most $C\ell$.

[F3] For every nonnegative measurable $q$, the map $E\mapsto\int_E q$ is a measure, hence finitely additive on disjoint measurable cells ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]). Nonnegative Lebesgue integrals preserve bounds ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); a constant bound integrates as that constant times the interval length ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: a continuous function on the compact interval $[0,1]$ has a finite maximum and minimum.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a cell $K=[a,b]=[x_j,x_{j+1}]$ of length $h_K$. Its interpolant slope is $s_K=(u(b)-u(a))/h_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^bu'(t)\,dt$ by [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 For every $x\in K$, $u'(x)-s_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^b(u'(x)-u'(t))\,dt$. A second use of [F1] and then [F2] gives $|u'(x)-u'(t)|\le\|u''\|_\infty|x-t|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$, hence $|u'(x)-s_K|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The continuous function $|u''|$ has a finite maximum by [F4]. On each open cell $K^\circ=(x_j,x_{j+1})$, $q=|u'-s_K|^2$ is continuous and hence measurable; define $q=0$ at the finitely many nodes. This gives a nonnegative measurable representative of the squared derivative error, bounded by the finite cell bounds in step 2.1. The Lebesgue interval-measure and monotonicity facts in [F3] give $\int_K|(u-I_hu)'|^2\le h_K^3\|u''\|_\infty^2$. The open cells are disjoint and their complement consists of finitely many nodes of Lebesgue measure zero. Finite additivity of the measure $E\mapsto\int_Eq$ from [F3], with zero contribution from the nodes where $q=0$, therefore identifies the global Lebesgue squared norm with the sum of these cell integrals. Using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_Kh_K=1$ gives $\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2^2\le h^2\|u''\|_\infty^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the estimate; endpoint values follow from the nodal definition. [F3, F4, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An arbitrary measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$; a nonnegative measurable function $f$.

[L1] The set function $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$ is defined by $A\mapsto\int f\chi_A\,d\mu$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[L2] Monotone convergence holds for the nonnegative integral ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

[L3] The nonnegative integral is additive on measurable sets ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L4] A measure must vanish at the empty set and be countably additive on disjoint measurable sequences ([[def-measure]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 One has $\nu_f(\varnothing)=0$. If $(A_n)$ is a pairwise disjoint sequence, put $B_n:=\bigcup_{k<n}A_k$. Then $\chi_{B_n}\uparrow\chi_{\bigcup_kA_k}$, so $f\chi_{B_n}\uparrow f\chi_{\bigcup_kA_k}$, including where $f=+\infty$ under the convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. By [L2], $\nu_f(\bigcup_kA_k)=\lim_n\nu_f(B_n)$. [L1, L2, given]

2.1 Because the sets $A_k$ are disjoint, $f\chi_{B_n}=\sum_{k<n}f\chi_{A_k}$. Repeated use of [L3] gives $\nu_f(B_n)=\sum_{k<n}\nu_f(A_k)$. Taking the increasing limit in step 1.1 proves countable additivity. [step 1.1, L3, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verify the two conditions in [L4], so $\nu_f$ is a measure. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An arbitrary measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$; nonnegative measurable functions $f,g$ and a scalar $c\ge0$.

[L1] The nonnegative integral is the supremum of simple minorants ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L2] On simple functions, the nonnegative and simple integrals agree ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[L3] The simple integral is homogeneous for positive scalars and has zero integral on the zero simple function ([[prop-basic-properties-of-the-nonnegative-simple-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $f\le g$, every simple minorant of $f$ is also a simple minorant of $g$. Taking suprema in [L1] gives $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. [L1, given]

1.2 The zero function has just one nonnegative simple minorant: itself. [L1, L2, L3] Its simple integral is $0$ by [L3], so [L1] gives integral $0$ for the zero function, even on a space of infinite measure. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 For $c>0$, multiplication by $c$ bijects simple minorants of $f$ with those of $cf$. The inverse divides by $c$ and preserves nonnegativity and simplicity. By [L2] and [L3], the corresponding simple integrals differ by the factor $c$. Multiplication by a positive finite real commutes with the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$, including when that supremum is infinite. Hence $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. Together with steps 1.1 and 1.2, this proves both clauses. [L1, given, algebra, L2, L3] ∎

## Statement

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonnegative simple measurable function $s$.

[L1] The nonnegative integral is the supremum of the simple integrals of all simple minorants $0\le u\le s$ ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L2] The simple integral is monotone on nonnegative simple functions ([[prop-basic-properties-of-the-nonnegative-simple-integral]]).

[L3] The simple integral itself is well defined on every nonnegative simple function ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The function $s$ is one of its own admissible simple minorants, so [L1] gives $$\int s\,d\mu\ge\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$ [given, L1, L3]

1.2 If $u$ is any admissible simple minorant of $s$, then $u\le s$, so [L2] gives $$\int_{\mathrm{simple}} u\,d\mu\le\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$ Taking the supremum over all such $u$ in [L1] yields the reverse inequality. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The two inequalities from steps 1.1 and 1.2 give equality of the nonnegative and simple integrals on $s$. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, reals $a_i \le b_i$ for $i<n$, and the sets $R^\circ$, $\overline{R}$ displayed in the Statement.

[L1] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra, $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it, every set of Lebesgue outer measure zero is Lebesgue measurable of measure zero, and $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[L3] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]), so it is monotone and countably subadditive ([[def-outer-measure]], [[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]).

[L4] For a nonempty box $\operatorname{vol}(B) := \prod_{i<n}(b_i - a_i)$ when every $a_i$ and every $b_i$ is real, and a box is nonempty exactly when $a_i < b_i$ for every $i < n$ ([[def-half-open-box]]).

[F1] $[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\}$ and $\operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[F2] A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive on pairwise disjoint sequences ([[def-measure]]).

[F3] For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $k \ge 1$ with $1/k < \varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[F4] $\prod_{k<n}(a_kb_k) = (\prod_{k<n}a_k)(\prod_{k<n}b_k)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k<n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, with $\prod_{k<n}a_k>0$ when every $a_k>0$; and finite products are defined by the recursion $\Pi_0 = 1$, $\Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claim 6; [[def-finite-sum]]).

[F5] A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$; a subset $F$ is **closed** if its complement is open ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F6] The forms $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are **half-open**, and an interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, **closed** when both are included ([[def-interval]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $R^{\circ}$ is open and $\overline{R}$ is closed in $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$, by the same coordinatewise estimate in each case, so both are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. [L2, F1, F5, F6]

1.2 A closed rectangle with a degenerate side is Lebesgue null: let $u_i \le v_i$ be reals with $u_{i_0} = v_{i_0} = c$ for some $i_0 < n$, and let $\eta$ be a positive real; the half-open box with parameter pairs $(u_i-1, v_i]$ for $i \ne i_0$ and $(c-\eta, c]$ in coordinate $i_0$ is nonempty, contains $[u,v]$, and has volume $\eta\,C$ where $C := \prod_{i<n}w_i > 0$ with $w_{i_0} := 1$ and $w_i := v_i-u_i+1$ otherwise, so monotonicity of the outer measure gives $\lambda_n^*([u,v]) \le \eta C$ for every positive real $\eta$ and hence $\lambda_n^*([u,v]) = 0$. [L1, L3, L4, F1, F3, F4]

2.1 The difference $\overline{R} \setminus R^{\circ}$ is contained in the union of the $2n$ closed rectangles obtained from $[a,b]$ by replacing the $i$-th side by the degenerate side $[a_i,a_i]$ or by $[b_i,b_i]$, each of which is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, so countable subadditivity of the outer measure, applied to that finite list padded with empty sets, gives $\lambda_n^*(\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}) = 0$; every subset of $\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}$ is therefore Lebesgue measurable of measure $0$. [step 1.2, L1, L3]

2.2 Suppose instead $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for some $i_0<n$. Then $R^{\circ} = \varnothing$, the rectangle $\overline{R}$ is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, every $R$ between them is a subset of it and so is measurable of measure $0$, and the product $\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$ has the factor $0$ and is therefore $0$ as well. [step 1.2, L1, F4]

3.1 Suppose first that $a_i < b_i$ for every $i<n$. Then $B(a,b)$ is a nonempty half-open box with $R^{\circ} \subseteq B(a,b) \subseteq \overline{R}$ and $\lambda_n(B(a,b)) = \operatorname{vol}(B(a,b)) = \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$. For $R$ with $R^{\circ}\subseteq R\subseteq\overline{R}$, both $R \setminus B(a,b)$ and $B(a,b)\setminus R$ are contained in $\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}$, hence are measurable of measure $0$ by step 2.1, so $R = \big(B(a,b)\setminus(B(a,b)\setminus R)\big)\cup\big(R\setminus B(a,b)\big)$ is measurable, and additivity on the two disjoint decompositions $R = (R\cap B(a,b)) \sqcup (R\setminus B(a,b))$ and $B(a,b) = (R\cap B(a,b)) \sqcup (B(a,b)\setminus R)$ gives $\lambda_n(R) = \lambda_n(R\cap B(a,b)) = \lambda_n(B(a,b))$. [step 2.1, L1, L4, F2]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 2.2 exhaust the two cases and give the displayed value in each, and step 1.1 supplies the Borel and measurability clauses for $R^{\circ}$ and $\overline{R}$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the geometry setting of [[def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy]], and suppose $\Omega_h$ has a nonempty finite measurable partition into bounded cells $\{K\}$, with $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and $h:=\max_Kh_K$. For real-valued $U,W\in C^1(\Omega)$ with $\nabla U,\nabla W\in L^2(\Omega)$, put $v:=U\circ\Phi_h$ and $w:=W\circ\Phi_h$, and assume their gradients are square-integrable on each cell. Then the physical exact form $a(U,W)$ pulled back by $\Phi_h$ is $a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)$. Suppose the implemented tensors $\widetilde B_h$ are real symmetric and measurable, with $\eta_{G,K}<\infty$. The form $\widetilde a_h(v,w):=\sum_K\int_K\nabla v^T\widetilde B_h\nabla w$ satisfies

$$|a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)-\widetilde a_h(v,w)|\le\sum_K\eta_{G,K}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(K)}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}\le\eta_G\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)},$$

where $\eta_G:=\max_K\eta_{G,K}$. If $\eta_{G,K}\le C_Gh_K^s$ for $s>0$, the form defect is at most $C_Gh^s\|\nabla v\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2$. Moreover, if $J_h\ge j_->0$, $0<L$, and $\|D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty,\mathrm{op}}\le L$, then $B_h\succeq\beta I$ with $\beta=j_-\lambda/L^2$. For the stability conclusion, let $Z_h$ be a real Hilbert space of pullback functions with inner product $\int_{\Omega_h}\nabla v\cdot\nabla w$, so its norm is $\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}$. Restrict the exact and implemented forms to $Z_h$. If $\eta_G\le\beta/2$, the implemented form is coercive on $Z_h$ with constant at least $\beta/2$. The rate assumption is separate from the lift; neither it nor completeness of the gradient-norm space follows from a lift alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the geometry definition; a nonempty finite measurable cell partition; physical functions $U,W$ and their pullbacks $v,w$ as stated; a real symmetric measurable tensor $A$ with $\lambda I\preceq A\preceq\Lambda I$; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with positive Jacobian; measurable symmetric implemented tensors $\widetilde B_h$ with finite cell discrepancies; and, for the coercivity conclusion, the real Hilbert space $Z_h$ with the gradient inner product specified in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy]]: $B_h=J_hD\Phi_h^{-1}(A\circ\Phi_h)D\Phi_h^{-T}$ and $\eta_{G,K}=\|B_h-\widetilde B_h\|_{L^\infty(K;\mathrm{op})}$.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: differentiating $U\circ\Phi_h$ gives $\nabla(U\circ\Phi_h)=D\Phi_h^T(\nabla U\circ\Phi_h)$, so $\nabla U\circ\Phi_h=D\Phi_h^{-T}\nabla(U\circ\Phi_h)$.

[F3] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes variables by the positive factor $J_h$ for every nonnegative measurable integrand.

[F4] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: integral Cauchy–Schwarz applies on each cell, and the finite sum of cell products is bounded by the product of the two Euclidean norms of the cellwise L2 norms.

[F5] [[lem-discrete-form-perturbation-preserves-coercivity]]: a diagonal perturbation bounded by $\eta\|v\|^2$ lowers a coercivity constant by at most $\eta$.

[F6] [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]: coercivity in a real Hilbert space means $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for every vector.

[F7] Nonnegative Lebesgue integration over measurable sets is a measure ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]), and the integral is linear on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). Finite products and sums of measurable real functions are measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

[A3] Countable Choice is the explicit assumption of the change-of-variables supplier [F3] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[A1] $J_h\ge j_->0$, $0<L$, and $\|D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty,\mathrm{op}}\le L$.

[A2] On each cell $K$, $\eta_{G,K}\le C_Gh_K^s$ for the stated optional rate conclusion.

## Proof

1.1 Set $v=U\circ\Phi_h$ and $w=W\circ\Phi_h$. By [F2], $\nabla U\circ\Phi_h=D\Phi_h^{-T}\nabla v$ and likewise for $W$. Under the Countable Choice hypothesis [A3], apply [F3] to the nonnegative measurable energy density $\nabla U^TA\nabla U$ to obtain $a(U,U)=a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,v)$; the same applies to $W$ and $U+W$. The physical energies are finite since $A\preceq\Lambda I$ and all three physical gradients are in $L^2$. Their nonnegative pulled-back energy densities therefore have finite integrals. The pointwise polarization identity expresses the pulled-back cross density as half the difference of these three integrable nonnegative densities, hence makes that cross density absolutely integrable. The physical cross density is integrable by the same argument. Since $A$ and $B_h$ are symmetric, the real polarization identity $2a(U,W)=a(U+W,U+W)-a(U,U)-a(W,W)$ yields $a(U,W)=a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)$. [F1, F2, F3, A3, given, algebra]

1.2 For every vector $\xi$, [A1] and $A\succeq\lambda I$ imply $\xi^TB_h\xi=J_h(D\Phi_h^{-T}\xi)^TA(\Phi_h)(D\Phi_h^{-T}\xi)\ge j_-\lambda\|D\Phi_h^{-T}\xi\|^2\ge(j_-\lambda/L^2)\|\xi\|^2$. Thus $B_h\succeq\beta I$. [F1, A1, given, algebra]

2.1 The finite measurable partition and the assumed finite cellwise squared-gradient integrals give global square integrability: apply the measure property [F7] to $|\nabla v|^2$ and $|\nabla w|^2$ to obtain $\|\nabla v\|_2^2=\sum_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(K)}^2$ and the analogous identity for $w$. The tensor and gradient entries are measurable, so the defect density $q=\nabla v^T(B_h-\widetilde B_h)\nabla w$ is measurable by [F7]. On each cell $|q|\le\eta_{G,K}|\nabla v||\nabla w|$ almost everywhere; [F4] makes this an integrable majorant, and the finite sum makes $q$ globally $L^1$. Step 1.1 has established that the exact lifted cross density is $L^1$. Thus the implemented cross density, the exact cross density minus $q$, is also $L^1$. Their finite indicator decompositions over the partition and $L^1$ linearity [F7] justify subtracting and summing cell integrals. The operator-norm estimate and integral Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] then give $|\int_K\nabla v^T(B_h-\widetilde B_h)\nabla w|\le\eta_{G,K}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(K)}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}$. Summing over cells and using $\eta_{G,K}\le\eta_G$ together with finite Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] proves both displayed form-defect bounds; under [A2], $\eta_G\le C_Gh^s$. [F1, F4, F7, A2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The diagonal estimate in step 2.1 has constant $\eta_G$. On $Z_h$, the exact lifted form is coercive with constant $\beta$ by step 1.2 and [F6]. Apply [F5] with $V=V_h=Z_h$ to obtain coercivity of the implemented form with constant at least $\beta-\eta_G\ge\beta/2$. [F5, F6, given, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integrable functions $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$.

[L1] Real and complex integrability, together with the decomposition into positive and negative parts and into real and imaginary parts, is defined in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

[L2] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L3] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[L4] Sums and real scalar multiples of measurable real-valued functions are measurable ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First treat real-valued $f,g$ and put $h:=f+g$. By [L4], the function $h$ is measurable. Also $$h^+\le f^++g^+,\qquad h^-\le f^-+g^-,$$ so [L2] and [L3] give $$\int h^+\,d\mu\le\int f^+\,d\mu+\int g^+\,d\mu<+\infty,\qquad \int h^-\,d\mu\le\int f^-\,d\mu+\int g^-\,d\mu<+\infty.$$ Hence $h$ is integrable. Since $$h^++f^-+g^-=h^-+f^++g^+,$$ another application of [L2] yields $$\int h^+\,d\mu+\int f^-\,d\mu+\int g^-\,d\mu =\int h^-\,d\mu+\int f^+\,d\mu+\int g^+\,d\mu,$$ which rearranges to $$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$ [L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

1.2 Now let $c\in\mathbb R$ and let $f$ be real-valued. By [L4], $cf$ is measurable. If $c\ge0$, then $$(cf)^+=cf^+,\qquad (cf)^-=cf^-;$$ if $c<0$, then $$(cf)^+=(-c)f^-,\qquad (cf)^-=(-c)f^+.$$ In both cases [L3] shows that $cf$ is integrable and that $$\int(cf)\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu.$$ [L1, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Let $h=u+iv\in L^1(\mu)$ and $\gamma=a+ib\in\mathbb C$. Then $$\gamma h=(au-bv)+i(av+bu).$$ The real-valued functions $au-bv$ and $av+bu$ are integrable by steps 1.1 and 1.2, and their real-linear integral formulas combine into $$\int(\gamma h)\,d\mu=\gamma\int h\,d\mu.$$ Writing $\alpha f=h_1+ik_1$ and $\beta g=h_2+ik_2$ with real-valued integrable $h_j,k_j$, step 1.1 gives $$\int(\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu =\int(h_1+h_2)\,d\mu+i\int(k_1+k_2)\,d\mu =\int h_1\,d\mu+i\int k_1\,d\mu+\int h_2\,d\mu+i\int k_2\,d\mu =\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu.$$ [L1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ and Borel-measurable functions $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$.

[L1] Measurability is equivalent to measurability of all strict upper (or lower) real threshold sets. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])

[L2] The parts are $h^+=\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\max(-h,0)$; $|h|=\max(h,-h)$. At every point one part is zero. ([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]])

[L3] Reflection reverses extended-real order. Partial addition excludes exactly the opposite-infinity pairs; addition with zero is defined. ([[def-extended-reals]])

[L4] The total function product $u\odot_X v$ is zero when either value is zero, is the real product on finite values, and otherwise is the infinity with the sign of the product. This includes all four ordered zero-infinity pairs. ([[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]])

[L5] A sigma-algebra contains $X$ and the empty set and is closed under finite intersections and countable unions; the rationals are countable, and between distinct real numbers lies a rational. ([[def-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-sigma-algebra-closure-laws]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]])

[L6] Finite real arithmetic is ordered-field arithmetic. ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Scalar multiples are measurable. If $c>0$, the product clauses give $\{cf>a\}=\{f>a/c\}$ for every real $a$, including infinite values of $f$. If $c<0$, they give $\{cf>a\}=\{f<a/c\}$. If $c=0$, $cf$ is constantly zero, whose threshold sets are $X$ or empty. Thus [L1] proves the claim, including measurability of $-f$. The latter agrees pointwise with reflection by the finite and the two infinite sign cases. [given, L1, L3, L4, L5, L6]

1.2 Assume $f+g$ is defined at every point. For every real $a$, $$\{f+g>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\bigl(\{f>q\}\cap\{g>a-q\}\bigr).$$ To check the right-to-left inclusion, both values then exceed finite bounds, hence neither is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$; otherwise finite ordered-field addition gives $f(x)+g(x)>a$. Conversely, a defined sum greater than $a$ cannot have a $-\infty$ summand. If both summands are finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<f(x)$. If $f(x)=+\infty$ and $g(x)$ is finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<a-g(x)+1$. If $g(x)=+\infty$ and $f(x)$ is finite, choose $f(x)-1<q<f(x)$. If both are $+\infty$, take $q=0$. These are all cases. The union is countable and each intersection is measurable, proving measurability of the sum. [L1, L3, L5, L6]

1.3 Let $u,v:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Their product is nonnegative by [L4], so its strict upper threshold set is $X$ when $a<0$. For real $a\ge0$, $$\{u\odot_X v>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}\bigl(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\}\bigr).$$ A point on the right has $u(x)>q>0$ and $v(x)>a/q\ge0$. If either value is infinite the product is $+\infty$; otherwise multiplying the strict finite bounds proves that the product exceeds $a$. Conversely, a product greater than $a\ge0$ has neither value zero. If both values are finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<u(x)$, which is possible because $u(x)v(x)>a$. If $u(x)$ is finite positive and $v(x)=+\infty$, choose $0<q<u(x)$. If $u(x)=+\infty$ and $v(x)$ is finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<a/v(x)+1$; this ensures $q>0$, also at $a=0$. If both values are $+\infty$, take $q=1$. These cases include $a=0$ and exclude zero-infinity pairs exactly because their product is zero. Countability and threshold measurability prove measurability of the nonnegative product. [L1, L4, L5, L6]

2.1 For real $a$, total order gives $$\{\max(f,g)>a\}=\{f>a\}\cup\{g>a\},\qquad \{\min(f,g)>a\}=\{f>a\}\cap\{g>a\}.$$ The threshold criterion gives measurability. The zero function is measurable, so this also gives measurability of $f^+$, $f^-$ and $|f|=\max(f,-f)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L5]

3.1 By step 2.1 the four parts $f^+,f^-,g^+,g^-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. Step 1.3 makes their four $\odot_X$ products measurable. Define $$h_+=(f^+\odot_X g^+)+(f^-\odot_X g^-),\qquad h_-=(f^+\odot_X g^-)+(f^-\odot_X g^+).$$ Each addition is defined because both summands are nonnegative, so step 1.2 proves that $h_+,h_-$ are measurable. If either original value is zero, all four products are zero. If both are positive, only $f^+\odot_X g^+$ can be nonzero; if both are negative, only $f^-\odot_X g^-$ can be nonzero. If $f(x)>0>g(x)$, only $f^+\odot_X g^-$ can be nonzero; if $f(x)<0<g(x)$, only $f^-\odot_X g^+$ can be nonzero. Thus at least one of $h_+(x),h_-(x)$ is zero in every case. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, L2, L3, L4]

4.1 The sum $h_++(-h_-)$ is therefore defined at every point. It is measurable by steps 1.1 and 1.2. status: draft

    - title: Joachim Schöberl, Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations, Chapter 25, Non-conforming Finite Element Methods
      url: https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/FEM/nonconforming.html

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ bounded and coercive, and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the exact Hilbert problem on $V$; the nonconforming space $V_h$ and common comparison norm on $X_h$; a bounded extension $\widetilde a_h$; discrete coercivity $\alpha_h>0$; and a bounded discrete load.

[F1] [[thm-lax-milgram]] under [[def-countable-choice]]: the exact bounded coercive Hilbert problem has a unique solution.

[F2] By definition, $\widetilde a_h$ agrees with $a_h$ on $V_h\times V_h$ and $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le M_h\|z\|_h\|w_h\|_h$ on $X_h\times V_h$ ([[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]).

[A1] $\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge\alpha_h\|v_h\|_h^2$ for every $v_h\in V_h$.

[A2] $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ is the consistency residual at the exact solution, as defined in [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]].

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] on $V$ to obtain the unique exact solution $u$. [F1, given]

1.2 The finite-dimensional Hilbert problem on $V_h$ has bounded coercive form $a_h$ and bounded load $F_h$, so the same Lax–Milgram theorem [F1] gives a unique $u_h\in V_h$. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 Fix $v_h\in V_h$ and set $e_h:=u_h-v_h$. Then $e_h\in V_h$, and [A1] gives $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h^2\le\operatorname{Re}a_h(e_h,e_h)=\operatorname{Re}(F_h(e_h)-\widetilde a_h(v_h,e_h))$. [A1, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 By the discrete equation and extension identity, $a_h(e_h,e_h)=\widetilde a_h(u-v_h,e_h)+F_h(e_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,e_h)$. The extension bound [F2] and residual definition [A2] therefore give $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h^2\le(M_h\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u))\|e_h\|_h$. [F2, A1, A2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $e_h=0$ there is nothing to divide by; otherwise divide step 3.1 by $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h$. The triangle inequality gives $\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h$. Taking the infimum over $v_h$ proves the per-mesh bound. For the stated family, replace $M_h/\alpha_h$ by $\overline M/\underline\alpha$ and $1/\alpha_h$ by $1/\underline\alpha$. The resulting constants are independent of $h$, yielding the stated uniform, convergence and rate consequences when the two explicit error terms have the corresponding control. [step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu \times \nu}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu \times \nu}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x\notin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y\notin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline\nu$ for $x\notin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y\notin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu \times \nu}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d\nu.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu \times \nu})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, two sigma-finite measure spaces, their completed product $\overline{\mu \times \nu}$, and either a nonnegative $\overline{\mu \times \nu}$-measurable function $f$ or an integrable function $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu \times \nu})$.

[L1] Assuming countable choice, a function measurable for a completion is almost everywhere equal to one measurable for the original sigma-algebra. ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]])

[L2] Tonelli and Fubini hold on the uncompleted product sigma-algebra. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[L3] Once both functions are integrable, the integral is unchanged by almost-everywhere equality. ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])

[L4] On a complete measure space, almost-everywhere equality with a measurable function implies measurability. ([[thm-ae-equality-preserves-measurability-on-complete-spaces]])

[L5] Integrable complex functions have integrable real and imaginary parts. ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]])

[L6] The nonnegative integral is the supremum over nonnegative simple minorants ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]); simple integrals are computed by finite level-set sums, independently of representation ([[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]]). A completed measurable set is $E=A\cup N$ with $A$ base measurable, $N$ contained in a base measurable null set, and $\overline\mu(E)=\mu(A)$ ([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]). A nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it is zero almost everywhere ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 We first justify two nonnegative transfer rules, allowing infinite integrals. On any measure space, if measurable $p,q\ge0$ agree outside a measurable null set $Z$, take a nonnegative simple $s\le p$ and replace each positive level set $E_j$ by $E_j\setminus Z$, assigning zero on $Z$. The resulting simple $s_0$ is bounded by $q$ and has the same integral as $s$, since removing a measurable null set does not change a level-set measure. Zero coefficients contribute zero even on infinite-measure sets by [L6]. Taking suprema of simple minorants gives $\int p\le\int q$; reversing them gives equality, without assuming finiteness. Also, for a base-measurable $p\ge0$, its integral is unchanged on completion: every base simple minorant is a completed one, while for a completed simple minorant $s=\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{E_j}\le p$, [L6] supplies base sets $A_j\subseteq E_j$ with $\mu(A_j)=\overline\mu(E_j)$. Taking the disjoint level-set representation makes the $A_j$ disjoint. The base simple function $s_0=\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}\le s\le p$ has the same integral; the two suprema are therefore equal. Only finitely many representatives are needed for any one simple function. These rules also give agreement of the signed or complex integrals on passing to completion once the absolute integral is finite, by applying them to the positive and negative real and imaginary parts in [L5]. [L5, L6, given, algebra]

1.2 In the nonnegative branch, [L1] gives a product-measurable extended-real function $g$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere for $\overline{\mu \times \nu}$. Let $N:=\{(x,y): f(x,y)\ne g(x,y)\}$, so $\overline{\mu \times \nu}(N)=0$. By the completion definition, choose a product-measurable null set $Z$ with $N \subseteq Z$. [L1, choose]

2.1 Apply Tonelli in [L2] to $\mathbf 1_Z$. Since $(\mu \times \nu)(Z)=0$, it gives $$\int_X \nu(Z_x)\,d\mu = 0,\qquad \int_Y \mu(Z^y)\,d\nu = 0.$$ The functions $x\mapsto\nu(Z_x)$ and $y\mapsto\mu(Z^y)$ are measurable, so $A:=\{x:\nu(Z_x)>0\}$ and $B:=\{y:\mu(Z^y)>0\}$ are measurable null sets by the zero-integral criterion in [L6]. For $x\notin A$, $f_x=g_x$ outside the null section $Z_x$; [L4] makes $f_x$ measurable for the completed factor measure. The analogous statement holds for $y\notin B$. [L2, L4, L6, step 1.2]

3.1 In the nonnegative case replace $g$ by $g^+=\max(g,0)$. Since $f\ge0$ and $f=g$ outside $Z$, one has $f=g^+$ there, both on the product and on sections outside $A,B$. Apply uncompleted Tonelli [L2] to $g^+$, with its base-measurable section-integral functions $I_g,J_g$. For each $x\notin A$, step 1.1 first transfers the section integral of $g^+$ to the completed factor and then transfers it to the equal-almost-everywhere $f_x$; thus $I_f(x)=I_g(x)$, and likewise $J_f=J_g$ outside $B$. The definitions set $I_f=0$ on the base-measurable set $A$ and $J_f=0$ on $B$, so these are base-measurable functions obtained by measurable piecewise gluing, not by an unqualified almost-everywhere measurability assertion on an incomplete space. Step 1.1 gives equal outer nonnegative integrals despite possible infinity, and also $\int f\,d\overline{\mu\times\nu}=\int g^+\,d(\mu\times\nu)$. Tonelli gives the asserted three-way equality. [L2, L4, L6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 If $f\in L^1(\overline{\mu\times\nu})$, apply [L1] separately to its finite real and imaginary parts, obtaining base-measurable extended-real $u,v$ equal to them almost everywhere. Their nonfinite sets are base measurable and null, because the completed measure extends the base measure; set $u,v$ to zero there and put $g=u+iv$. By completion there is a base-measurable null cover $Z$ of $\{f\ne g\}$. Applying the nonnegative rules of step 1.1 to $|f|,|g|$ gives $\int|g|\,d(\mu\times\nu)=\int|f|\,d\overline{\mu\times\nu}<\infty$, so $g$ is in base $L^1$ before invoking Fubini or [L3]. Fubini [L2] gives base-measurable null exceptional parameter sets for the integrability of its sections. Enlarge them by the null-section exceptional sets obtained from $Z$ as in step 2.1. Outside the enlarged $A,B$, [L4] makes the real and imaginary $f$ sections measurable on the completed factor; step 1.1 applied to absolute values shows their integrals finite, so both sections are integrable before [L3] equates their integrals. Step 1.1 also identifies the base and completed integrals of each integrable $g$ section. Hence $I_f,J_f$ equal the base Fubini section functions outside the base-measurable null sets $A,B$ and are zero on those sets. Piecewise gluing makes them base measurable, and step 1.1 applied to their absolute values proves integrability. Now [L3] equates the outer integrals; on the completed product, $f$ and $g$ are already integrable and equal almost everywhere, so [L3] followed by completion agreement in step 1.1 equates their product integrals as well. This proves the stated equality in the real and complex cases. [L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
