## Example

For the linear time-response model $F_t(\theta)=\theta_0+\theta_1t$ with candidate sensor times $t\in\{0,1,2\}$ and unit precision, the equal-weight endpoint design is D-optimal. Starting from uniform weights and using a one-update budget, the multiplicative procedure returns a positive equivalence violation instead of claiming exact optimality.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Candidate features $f_t=(1,t)^T$ at $t=0,1,2$, parameter dimension $p=2$, unit precision, and initial approximate design $\xi^{(0)}=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ in that order.

[F1] [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]: $M(\xi)=\sum_t\xi_tf_tf_t^T$ and D-optimality maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$ among nonsingular approximate designs.

[F2] [[alg-finite-budget-multiplicative-d-optimal-design]]: with $s_t=f_t^TM^{-1}f_t$, the update is $\xi_t^+=\xi_ts_t/p$ and the returned violation is $\max_ts_t-p$.

[F3] [[thm-multiplicative-design-update-well-defined-and-terminates]]: each exact update preserves the approximate-design simplex and nonsingularity.

[F4] [[thm-equivalence-violation-bounds-d-optimal-design-gap]]: zero violation certifies D-optimality, and a positive violation bounds every nonsingular competitor's log-determinant gap.

[F5] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] gives $\log'(x)=1/x>0$ for $x>0$. For $0<a<b$, the logarithm is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable inside, so [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] gives $\log b-\log a=(b-a)/c>0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$. Thus $\log$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

## Verification

1.1 For an arbitrary approximate design $\xi$, write $\mu=\sum_t\xi_tt$ and $\nu=\sum_t\xi_tt^2$. Direct multiplication gives $M(\xi)=\begin{bmatrix}1&\mu\\\mu&\nu\end{bmatrix}$ and $\det M(\xi)=\nu-\mu^2$. Since $0\le t\le2$, $(t-1)^2\le1$, so $\nu-\mu^2=\sum_t\xi_t(t-1)^2-(\mu-1)^2\le1$. The equal endpoint design $\xi^*=(1/2,0,1/2)$ has $M(\xi^*)=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and determinant $1$, so it maximizes the determinant and hence $\log\det M$ among nonsingular designs because $\log$ is strictly increasing by [F5]. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

1.2 For $\xi^{(0)}$, $M_0=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&5/3\end{bmatrix}$ and $M_0^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}5/2&-3/2\\-3/2&3/2\end{bmatrix}$. Thus $(s_0,s_1,s_2)=(5/2,1,5/2)$ and $v_0=1/2$. 2.1 The updated matrix is $M_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&11/6\end{bmatrix}$, with inverse $M_1^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}11/5&-6/5\\-6/5&6/5\end{bmatrix}$. [step 1.2, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 For the endpoint design $\xi^*$, $M(\xi^*)^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, so its sensitivities at $0,1,2$ are $2,1,2$ and its violation is zero. By [F4] this is an exact D-optimality certificate; [F4] also bounds the log-determinant gap of the one-update output by $1/5$. The weights are approximate-design weights; integer run counts are a separate problem by [F1]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $p\ge1$, if $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ are symmetric and $v^{\mathsf T}A_i v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and $i\in\{0,1\}$, then for every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)\ge(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two real symmetric positive-definite $p\times p$ matrices $A_0,A_1$, with $p\ge1$.

[F1] [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]: the standard pairing on $\mathbb R^p$ is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<p}x_i y_i$.

[F2] [[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]]: $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$; over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is $A^{\mathsf T}$.

[F3] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F4] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

[F5] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: for same-sized square matrices over a commutative ring, $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.

[F6] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]: $\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}$.

[F7] [[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]: $d(AB)=dA\,B+A\,dB$.

[F8] [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]: on the invertible locus, $D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H)$.

[F9] [[thm-derivative-of-matrix-inversion]]: for invertible $A$, $D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$.

[F10] [[prop-differentials-of-trace-and-frobenius-linear-functionals]]: $D(\operatorname{tr})(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H)$.

[F11] [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]: $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$.

[F12] [[def-matrix-minors-cofactors-and-adjugate]]: for a positive-sized square matrix, the cofactors are signed deleted-row-and-column minors and $\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A)^{\mathsf T}$.

[F13] [[thm-laplace-cofactor-expansion]]: for a positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, determinant expansion along any row or column is the sum of entries times their corresponding cofactors.

[F14] [[thm-adjugate-identity-over-a-commutative-ring]]: for a positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)A=\det(A)I$.

[F15] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log'(x)=1/x$ for $x>0$. Under the entrywise identification of a real matrix space with a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] composes its Fréchet derivatives with the scalar logarithm and an affine matrix path. The path $t\mapsto A_0+tH$ has derivative $H$ and zero remainder.

[F16] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior has an increment equal to the interval length times an interior derivative.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** restrict to a line and compute its second derivative.

1.1 For $t\in[0,1]$, put $A_t=(1-t)A_0+tA_1$ and $H=A_1-A_0$. For every nonzero $v$, $v^{\mathsf T}A_tv=(1-t)v^{\mathsf T}A_0v+t v^{\mathsf T}A_1v>0$, so $A_t$ is symmetric positive definite. By [F1] the standard coordinate basis is orthonormal, [F2] makes the symmetric matrix self-adjoint, and [F3] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each eigenvalue $\lambda_i(t)$ is positive because for its unit eigenvector $v_i$, $\lambda_i(t)=v_i^{\mathsf T}A_tv_i>0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 In that eigenbasis $A_t=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$ with $Q Q^{\mathsf T}=I_p$ and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1(t),\ldots,\lambda_p(t))$. By [F4] and [F5], $\det A_t=\det Q\,\det\Lambda\,\det Q^{\mathsf T}=\det\Lambda=\prod_i\lambda_i(t)>0$, since [F5] gives $\det Q\det Q^{\mathsf T}=\det I_p$ and [F6] gives $\det I_p=1$ from the Leibniz formula. Thus $g(t)=\log\det A_t$ is real-valued on $[0,1]$. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $A_t$ is invertible, the determinant differential in [F8] is Jacobi's formula; its cofactor representation and invertible-matrix reduction use [F12], [F13], and [F14]. Because the determinant is differentiable, it is continuous; its positive value at each $A_t$ remains positive on a small neighborhood of that path point, so the logarithm's domain condition in [F15] is met, including at $t=0,1$. The logarithm derivative and total chain rule [F15] then give $g'(t)=(\det A_t)^{-1}D\det(A_t)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(A_t^{-1}H)$. [F8, F12, F13, F14, F15, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Differentiate this trace along the same line. The product rule [F7], inverse derivative [F9], and trace derivative [F10], composed with the affine path by [F15], give $g''(t)=-\operatorname{tr}(A_t^{-1}H A_t^{-1}H)$. [F7, F9, F10, F15, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix $t$ and define the symmetric matrix $S=A_t^{-1/2}HA_t^{-1/2}$ by diagonalizing $A_t$ from [F3] and taking the positive inverse square roots of its eigenvalues. By [F11], $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ because both sides are $\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ji}$ with indices interchanged; applying this identity gives $\operatorname{tr}(A_t^{-1}HA_t^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(S^2)=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}^2\ge0$. Hence [step 4.1] implies $g''(t)\le0$. [F3, F11, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The formulas in steps 3.1–4.1 make $g$ differentiable on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$ and $g'$ differentiable there; in particular each is continuous on the closed subintervals used below. For $0\le r<s\le1$, apply [F16] to $g'$ on $[r,s]$; step 5.1 gives $g'(s)-g'(r)=g''(c)(s-r)\le0$ for some $c\in(r,s)$. Thus $g'$ is nonincreasing. If $0<t<1$, apply [F16] to $g$ on $[0,t]$ and $[t,1]$. The respective slopes equal $g'(a)$ and $g'(b)$ for $a<t<b$, hence $(g(t)-g(0))/t\ge(g(1)-g(t))/(1-t)$. Rearrangement gives $g(t)\ge(1-t)g(0)+tg(1)$. At $t=0,1$ it is equality. This is precisely the stated log-determinant chord inequality. [F16, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$, and let $\xi^*$ be a nonsingular approximate design as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Write $M^*=M(\xi^*)$ and $u^*(x)=f(x)^{\mathsf T}(M^*)^{-1}f(x)$. Then $\xi^*$ is D-optimal among nonsingular approximate designs if and only if $u^*(x)\le p$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$. Whenever this holds, $u^*(x)=p$ for every $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi^*)$. No existence of a nonsingular optimum is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, a regression-vector map $f$, a nonsingular approximate design $\xi^*$, and its matrix $M^*$.

[F1] [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]: $M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}$ for an approximate design $\xi$.

[F2] [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]: D-optimality maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$ among nonsingular designs.

[F3] [[lem-log-determinant-concavity-on-positive-definite-matrices]]: for positive-definite $A_0,A_1$, $\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)\ge(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1$ for $0\le t\le1$.

[F4] [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]: for invertible $A$, $D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H)$.

[F5] [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]: $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$.

[F6] [[def-matrix-minors-cofactors-and-adjugate]]: for a positive-sized square matrix, the cofactors are signed deleted-row-and-column minors and $\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A)^{\mathsf T}$.

[F7] [[thm-laplace-cofactor-expansion]]: for a positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, determinant expansion along any row or column is the sum of entries times their corresponding cofactors.

[F8] [[thm-adjugate-identity-over-a-commutative-ring]]: for a positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)A=\det(A)I$.

[F9] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] gives $\log'(r)=1/r$ for $r>0$; [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] composes it with the determinant differential and affine matrix paths, using the entrywise Euclidean coordinates on real matrix space. Thus, along an affine path $A_t=A+tH$ with positive determinant, $(\log\det A_t)'=\operatorname{tr}(A_t^{-1}H)$ by [F4]. Determinant continuity keeps its positive value in the logarithm domain locally at every path point.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** use feasible directional derivatives for necessity and concavity for sufficiency.

1.1 Fix $x\in\mathcal X$ and let $\delta_x$ be the design putting weight $1$ at $x$. For $0\le t<1$, $\xi_t=(1-t)\xi^*+t\delta_x$ has matrix $M_t=(1-t)M^*+t f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}$, which is positive definite because $M^*$ is positive definite and $f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}$ is positive semidefinite. [given, F1, choose, algebra]

1.2 Conversely, suppose $u^*(x)\le p$ for every candidate. Let $\eta$ be any nonsingular approximate design and put $N=M(\eta)$. The segment $M_s=(1-s)M^*+sN$ is positive definite; by [F3], $g(s)=\log\det M_s$ is concave. By [F4], with its cofactor and adjugate support [F6], [F7], and [F8], and the logarithm-chain rule [F9], and by [F1], $g'(0)=\operatorname{tr}((M^*)^{-1}(N-M^*))=\sum_x\eta_x u^*(x)-p\le0$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, F9, choose, algebra]

2.1 If $\xi^*$ is D-optimal, the defining maximum property in [F2] gives $g_x(t)=\log\det M_t\le g_x(0)$ for $0\le t<1$, so its right derivative at $0$ is nonpositive. By [F4], with its cofactor and adjugate support [F6], [F7], and [F8], the logarithm-chain rule [F9] gives $g_x'(0)=\operatorname{tr}((M^*)^{-1}(f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}-M^*))=u^*(x)-p$; the trace of the rank-one term is $f(x)^{\mathsf T}(M^*)^{-1}f(x)$ by the coordinate sum, and $\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$ by [F5]. Thus $u^*(x)\le p$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, the pointwise bound is necessary. [given, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

2.2 For $0<s<1$, the concavity in step 1.2 gives $g(s)\ge(1-s)g(0)+sg(1)$, hence $g(1)-g(0)\le(g(s)-g(0))/s$. Let $s\downarrow0$; the right derivative already computed in step 1.2 gives $g(1)-g(0)\le g'(0)\le0$. Thus $\log\det N\le\log\det M^*$. Since $\eta$ was arbitrary among nonsingular designs, $\xi^*$ is D-optimal. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Finally, $\sum_x\xi_x^*u^*(x)=\operatorname{tr}((M^*)^{-1}\sum_x\xi_x^*f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$ by [F1] and [F5]. Each term is at most $p$ by the bound assumed in step 1.2, so every term with $\xi_x^*>0$ equals $p$. This proves equality on the support and completes both directions. [F1, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$ and a function $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$.

[L1] Cauchy's mean value theorem ([[thm-cauchy-mean-value]]): for $f, g$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)g'(c) = \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)f'(c)$.

[L2] The identity $x \mapsto x$ is continuous at every point of any $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], claim 5).

[L3] The identity $g$ on $[a,b]$ is differentiable at every $c \in [a,b]$ with $g'(c) = 1$: with $a < b$ the set $[a,b]$ is order-convex with at least two elements, so every one of its points is a limit point of it ([[def-derivative]], [[def-interval]]); and the difference quotient of $g$ at $c$ is $(x - c)/(x - c) = 1$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ with $x \ne c$, a constant function, whose limit at $c$ is $1$ ([[def-function-limit]], [[def-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g(x) := x$. [construct]

2.1 $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ by [L2]; it is differentiable at every $c \in (a,b)$ with $g'(c) = 1$ by [L3]; and $g(b) - g(a) = b - a$. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

3.1 By step 2.1 the pair $f, g$ satisfies every hypothesis of [L1], so there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)g'(c) = \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)f'(c)$. Substituting $g'(c) = 1$ and $g(b)-g(a) = b-a$ gives $f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b-a)$. [step 2.1, L1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The geometric reading, and what it is not.** The conclusion says that some tangent line is parallel to the chord from $(a, f(a))$ to $(b, f(b))$. It does not say which one, it does not say there is only one, and it says nothing at all about $f$ between the endpoints beyond the hypotheses. Every use of the theorem on this page is a use of the equation, never of the picture.

- **Why this is a corollary and not the primitive statement.** [[thm-cauchy-mean-value]] is proved from [[thm-rolle]] with one auxiliary function, and this statement is that theorem at $g(x) = x$; deriving it the other way round, from this statement to Cauchy's, is also possible but needs an auxiliary function of its own, so nothing is saved. What matters is that both rest on Rolle, and Rolle on the extreme value theorem.

- **The two hypotheses are on different sets on purpose.** Continuity is asked for on the closed interval and differentiability only on the open one, so nothing at all is required of the difference quotients at $a$ and at $b$. Weakening the continuity in step with the differentiability, so that both are asked for on $(a,b)$ only, destroys the theorem, which is exactly what [[cex-mean-value-theorem-fails-without-continuity-at-the-endpoints]] shows on the companion page.

## Statement

Gradients of scalar functions are Euclidean column vectors, with $Dg(\theta)[v]=\langle\nabla g(\theta),v\rangle$ under [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; vector expectations are taken coordinatewise.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$, and choose an open ball $U$ with $\theta_0\in U\subseteq\Theta$. Let $d,m\ge1$, let $N\ge0$ be a finite integer, let the states lie in $\mathbb R^m$, and let $\xi=(\xi_0,\ldots,\xi_N)$ collect fixed simulation inputs on one probability space. The maps are $u_0:\Theta\times E_0\to\mathbb R^m$, $\Psi_k:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\times E_{k+1}\to\mathbb R^m$, $\ell_k:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, and $\phi:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$. Gradients of scalar functions are columns; $D_u\Psi_k$ is an $m\times m$ Jacobian and $D_\theta\Psi_k$ is an $m\times d$ Jacobian. Let
$u_0=u_0(\theta,\xi_0),\qquad u_{k+1}=\Psi_k(u_k,\theta,\xi_{k+1})\quad(0\le k<N).$
Assume the displayed step data maps are jointly measurable in all their arguments and, outside one probability-zero set, are continuously differentiable in their state and parameter variables on $U$. Define
$F_N(\theta,\xi):=\phi(u_N,\theta)+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\ell_k(u_k,\theta),\qquad J_N(\theta):=\mathbb E[F_N(\theta,\xi)].$
Assume $F_N(\theta,\xi)$ is integrable for every $\theta\in U$, and that there is a nonnegative integrable random variable $M$ with $\|\nabla_\theta F_N(\theta,\xi)\|_2\le M$ for all $\theta\in U$ almost surely, while $\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta F_N(\theta_0,\xi)\|_2^2<\infty$. Put $S_0=D_\theta u_0$, propagate
$S_{k+1}=D_u\Psi_k\,S_k+D_\theta\Psi_k,$
and define reverse variables by
$p_N=\nabla_u\phi(u_N,\theta),\qquad p_k=\nabla_u\ell_k(u_k,\theta)+(D_u\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1}.$
Then the discrete adjoint integrand
$\Gamma_N=\nabla_\theta\phi+S_0^\mathsf T p_0+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\nabla_\theta\ell_k+(D_\theta\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1}\right)$
satisfies $\nabla J_N(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma_N(\theta_0,\xi)]$.

For a family of discretizations indexed by $h$, if each discrete objective satisfies the preceding pathwise interchange hypotheses, $\mathbb E\|\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)\|_2\to0$, and the continuous-limit objective has derivative $\nabla J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma(\theta_0)]$ under the same pathwise interchange conditions, then $\nabla J_h(\theta_0)\to\nabla J(\theta_0)$. This conclusion gives no rate unless a quantitative bound on $\mathbb E\|\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)\|_2$ is also supplied. Euler–Maruyama is the special case $\Psi_k(u,\theta,\Delta W_k)=u+b(u,\theta)h_k+\sigma(u,\theta)\Delta W_k$, with $\Delta W_k$ the simulated Brownian increment.

All tangent, reverse and adjoint derivatives are evaluated on the common full-probability event where the sample maps are $C^1$. Define $\Gamma_N=0$ on its measurable null complement, and use this version in expectations.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite simulation graph, its differentiability and pathwise envelope hypotheses, and, for the final convergence assertion, $L^1$ convergence of the discrete adjoint integrands and the stated derivative representation of the continuous-limit objective.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of compositions of differentiable Euclidean maps are obtained by composing their total derivatives.

[F2] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at the initial index and inherited at each successor holds at every finite index.

[F3] [[thm-pathwise-simulation-gradient-is-unbiased-under-envelope]]: an integrable common envelope for a continuous pathwise gradient allows differentiation of its expected objective, with derivative equal to the expected pathwise derivative.

[F4] [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: each $\xi_k$ is a measurable random element. A constant parameter map is measurable because each measurable-set preimage is either empty or the whole probability space.

[F5] [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]: for a finite deterministic $C^1$ state-step graph, the tangent and reverse recursions in the Statement give its exact objective gradient.

[F6] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: the composite of two measurable maps is measurable once the inner map is measurable into the outer map's measurable domain.

[F7] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, and $\|z\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\langle v,z\rangle$ (equality is attained by $v=z/\|z\|_2$ when $z\ne0$).

[F8] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: expectation is linear for integrable scalar random variables.

[F9] [[lem-coordinate-maps-and-permutations-are-measurable-on-finite-products]]: a finite tuple of measurable coordinate maps is measurable into the finite product sigma-algebra.

[F10] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: finite sums, differences, real scalar multiples and products of finite real measurable functions are measurable.

[F11] [[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]: a pointwise limit of a sequence of measurable functions is measurable.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $\vartheta\in U$. By [F4] the constant map $\omega\mapsto\vartheta$ and each $\xi_k$ are measurable. The finite-tuple lemma [F9] first makes $\omega\mapsto(\vartheta,\xi_0(\omega))$ measurable; joint measurability of the initial-state map and composition [F6] then make $u_0(\vartheta,\xi_0)$ measurable. If $u_k$ is measurable, [F9] makes $\omega\mapsto(u_k(\omega),\vartheta,\xi_{k+1}(\omega))$ measurable into the step map's finite product domain, and [F6] makes $u_{k+1}$ measurable. Finite induction [F2] gives every state. Applying [F9] and [F6] to $(u_k,\vartheta)$ in each payoff map and then [F10] to the finite sum proves measurability of $F_N(\vartheta,\xi)$, also when $N=0$. Let $A$ be the common measurable null set excluded in the Statement. Fix a coordinate $j$ and put $h_n=1/(n+1)$ for $n\ge0$. If $\vartheta+h_ne_j\in U$, form the measurable difference quotient $Q_{j,n}=(F_N(\vartheta+h_ne_j,\xi)-F_N(\vartheta,\xi))/h_n$; otherwise put $Q_{j,n}=0$. Measurability follows from the fixed-parameter argument and [F10]. Replace each $Q_{j,n}$ by zero on $A$: equivalently multiply it by the measurable indicator of $A^c$, which remains measurable by [F10]. Since $U$ is open, these modified quotients converge at every outcome to the version of $\partial_jF_N(\vartheta,\xi)$ given by its derivative on $A^c$ and zero on $A$. If $u_k$ is differentiable, [F1] applied to $u_{k+1}=\Psi_k(u_k,\theta_0,\xi_{k+1})$ gives $D_\theta u_{k+1}=D_u\Psi_k\,D_\theta u_k+D_\theta\Psi_k$. 2.1 Applying the chain rule to $F_N$ at $\theta_0$ gives its pathwise gradient $\nabla_\theta F_N=\nabla_\theta\phi+S_N^\mathsf T p_N+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\nabla_\theta\ell_k+S_k^\mathsf T\nabla_u\ell_k\right),$ where $p_N=\nabla_u\phi$. [given, F1, step 1.1]

## Statement

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The total first-order expansions of $f$ at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$.

[L1] In the total-derivative definition, the normalized remainder tends to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r_f(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)=g(f(a))+Dg(f(a))k+r_g(k)$, with both normalized remainders tending to zero. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], $k=f(a+h)-f(a)=O(\|h\|_2)$; boundedness of $Dg(f(a))$ and the two remainder limits show both $Dg(f(a))r_f(h)$ and $r_g(k)$ are $o(\|h\|_2)$, including the case $k=0$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Substitution into the two expansions leaves $g(f(a+h))-g(f(a))-Dg(f(a))Df(a)h=o(\|h\|_2)$, and the composite of linear maps is linear. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathbb{N} = \omega$ is the smallest inductive set ([[def-inductive-set]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]); $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$.

[L1] $\omega$ is contained in every inductive set ([[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $0 = \varnothing \in S$ and ($x \in S \Rightarrow \sigma(x) = x \cup \{x\} \in S$). [given]

2.1 Then $S$ contains $\varnothing$ and is closed under $x \mapsto x \cup \{x\}$, so $S$ is an inductive set. [step 1.1]

3.1 $\mathbb{N} = \omega \subseteq S$ because $\omega$ is a subset of every inductive set. [L1, step 2.1]

4.1 With $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ by hypothesis, $S = \mathbb{N}$. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 The property form is the set case with $S = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : P(n)\}$: $P(0)$ and $P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$ give $0 \in S$ and $\sigma$-closure, so $S = \mathbb{N}$, i.e. $P$ holds for all $n$; conversely the set form is the property form applied to $P(n) :\equiv n \in S$, so the two are equivalent. [step 4.1] ∎
",

## Statement

Gradients are Euclidean column vectors, and vector expectations are taken coordinatewise.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $H:\Theta\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the simulation payoff from [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]], and fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Suppose there is an open ball $U$ about $\theta_0$ such that for almost every $\omega$, $H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuously differentiable on $U$ and $\nabla_\theta H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuous there, and $\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\cdot)$ is measurable for every $\theta\in U$. Assume $\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega)\|_2\le M(\omega)$ for all $\theta\in U$ outside one measurable null set, where $M$ is nonnegative and integrable, and assume $\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)\|_2^2<\infty$. Then $J(\theta)=\mathbb E H(\theta,\cdot)$ is Fréchet differentiable at $\theta_0$ and
$\nabla J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)].$
Thus the pathwise estimator from [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]] is unbiased at $\theta_0$ and has finite coordinate variances.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The payoff and objective, $\theta_0$, the neighborhood and pathwise differentiability, the common integrable derivative envelope, and the square-integrable pathwise gradient in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]]: when the same random input is held fixed, the pathwise estimator is $D_\theta H(\theta,Z)$; the definition by itself does not assert unbiasedness.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for a differentiable composition, $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. Gradients are column vectors represented using the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], so $D_\theta H(\theta,\omega)[h]=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega),h\rangle$.

[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: if $q'$ is continuous on a compact interval, it is integrable there and $\int_a^b q'(t)\,dt=q(b)-q(a)$.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and [[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]]: for square-integrable $X$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb E X)^2\le\mathbb E[X^2]$.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $h\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\theta_0+h\in U$. For almost every $\omega$, set $q_\omega(t)=H(\theta_0+th,\omega)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F2], $q_\omega'(t)=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega),h\rangle$, which is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. The FTC [F3] gives
$H(\theta_0+h,\omega)-H(\theta_0,\omega)-\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle=\int_0^1\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle\,dt.$ [given, F2, F3]

1.2 For each such $h$, the random variable $M_h(\omega):=\sup_{r\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+rh,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega)\|_2$ is measurable: continuity in $t$ makes this countable supremum equal the supremum over $[0,1]$. It satisfies $0\le M_h\le2M$ almost surely. As $h\to0$, continuity of the sample gradient at $\theta_0$ gives $M_h\to0$ almost surely. [given, F1]

2.1 Taking expectations in step 1.1 and using [F6] bounds the absolute first-order remainder divided by $\|h\|_2$ by $\mathbb E M_h$. Along every sequence $h_n\to0$, [F4] with majorant $2M$ gives $\mathbb E M_{h_n}\to0$. Hence $J(\theta_0+h)-J(\theta_0)-\langle\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)],h\rangle=o(\|h\|_2),$ which is the Fréchet derivative formula. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4, F6, algebra]

3.1 Each coordinate of the unbiased estimator is square-integrable by the stated second-moment assumption. [F5] therefore gives finite variance for each coordinate. [given, F1, F5, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open finite state-step graph, its $C^1$ maps, objective, trajectory and parameter in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]: $x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$ and $J=\phi(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n<N}\ell_n(x_n,\theta)$ with all displayed maps $C^1$.

[F2] [[alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiation]]: reverse mode accumulates each primitive pullback $D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$ at every parent slot in reverse topological order.

[F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: reverse mode returns the exact gradient of the finite $C^1$ real-arithmetic graph.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition. [F1, F4]

1.2 Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measurable spaces $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, $(Z,\mathcal{C})$, a measurable map $f : X \to Y$, and a measurable map $g : Y \to Z$.

[L1] Measurability means that preimages of measurable sets are measurable. ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $C \in \mathcal{C}$. Since $g$ is measurable, [L1] gives $g^{-1}(C) \in \mathcal{B}$. [given, L1]

2.1 Since $f$ is measurable, [L1] applied again gives $$(g \circ f)^{-1}(C) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C)) \in \mathcal{A}.$$ So $g \circ f$ is measurable. [step 1.1, L1] ∎",

## Definition

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

## Remarks

- **Scope: the concrete form only.** What is defined above is the Euclidean inner
  product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and nothing more. The general theory of inner
  product spaces — abstract inner products, orthonormal bases, Gram-Schmidt,
  orthogonal projection and orthogonal complements of arbitrary subspaces — is
  developed elsewhere in this library. No item on this page claims anything about abstract inner
  product spaces, and no item on this page introduces the general notion.

- **The standard basis and coordinates.** For $i < n$ the standard unit vector
  $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ has $e_i(i) = 1$ and $e_i(j) = 0$ for $j \ne i$
  ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). Then $\langle x, e_i\rangle = x_i$: the list
  $k \mapsto x_k (e_i)_k$ vanishes except at $k = i$, where its value is $x_i$,
  and a list vanishing off one index sums to its value there
  ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 3, splitting the range at $i$). So the
  coordinates of $x$ are recovered by testing against the standard basis, which
  is the form used repeatedly below.

- **Powers here are integer powers.** $x_k^{2}$ means the integer power of
  [[def-integer-power]], and $\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} = \langle x,x\rangle$ by
  [[thm-of-square-roots]] and [[lem-power-laws]].

## Statement

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n$ and vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, so that $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L1] Cauchy-Schwarz for finite sums ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]): $\bigl(\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k\bigr)^{2} \le \bigl(\sum_{k<n}a_k^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<n}b_k^{2}\bigr)$, with equality if and only if there is $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every $k<n$; and the root form $\bigl|\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k\bigr| \le \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}a_k^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}b_k^{2}}$.

[L2] The inner product is symmetric, bilinear and positive definite, $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n}x_k^{2} \ge 0$, and $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ exactly when $x = 0$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L3] Square roots ([[thm-of-square-roots]]): every $c \ge 0$ has a unique $s \ge 0$ with $s^{2} = c$, written $\sqrt{c}$; hence $\lVert x\rVert_2 \ge 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} = \langle x,x\rangle$ ([[def-integer-power]]).

[L4] Squaring is monotone on the nonnegatives: for $a,b \ge 0$, $a \le b$ if and only if $a^{2} \le b^{2}$, and $a = b$ if and only if $a^{2} = b^{2}$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[L5] Absolute value ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]): $|t| \ge 0$, $|t|^{2} = t^{2}$, and $|st| = |s|\,|t|$.

[L6] The norm axioms (N1), (N2), (N3) ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and the fact that $d_2(u,v) = \lVert u-v\rVert_2$ for $n \ge 1$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] clause 6).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Instantiating [L1] at $a_k := x_k$ and $b_k := y_k$ gives $\langle x,y\rangle^{2} \le \langle x,x\rangle\,\langle y,y\rangle$, with equality exactly when some $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ has $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k<n$. [L1, L2]

1.2 Both $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ are nonnegative, and their squares are $\langle x,y\rangle^{2}$ and $\langle x,x\rangle\langle y,y\rangle$. [L3, L5]

1.3 Expanding by bilinearity and symmetry, $\langle x+y, x+y\rangle = \langle x,x\rangle + \langle x,y\rangle + \langle y,x\rangle + \langle y,y\rangle = \lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\langle x,y\rangle + \lVert y\rVert_2^{2}$. [L2, L3]

1.4 The same expansion at $x - y = x + (-1)y$ gives $\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} = \lVert x\rVert_2^{2} - 2\langle x,y\rangle + \lVert y\rVert_2^{2}$. [L2, L3]

1.5 For a scalar $\lambda$, $\langle \lambda x, \lambda x\rangle = \lambda^{2}\langle x,x\rangle = |\lambda|^{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^{2}$, so $\lVert \lambda x\rVert_2^{2} = \bigl(|\lambda|\lVert x\rVert_2\bigr)^{2}$. [L2, L3, L5]

1.6 Axiom (N1) holds: $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$ if and only if $\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} = \langle x,x\rangle = 0$, which by positive definiteness says $x = 0$. [L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Comparing the squares of step 1.2 through step 1.1 and using monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives yields $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$, with equality exactly in the proportional case of step 1.1; this is clause 1. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L4]

2.2 Adding the identities of step 1.3 and step 1.4 gives $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} = 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2}$, which is clause 3. [step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

2.3 Subtracting the identity of step 1.4 from that of step 1.3 gives $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} = 4\langle x,y\rangle$, which is clause 4 after dividing by $4$. [step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

2.4 Both $\lVert \lambda x\rVert_2$ and $|\lambda|\lVert x\rVert_2$ are nonnegative and by step 1.5 have equal squares, so $\lVert \lambda x\rVert_2 = |\lambda|\lVert x\rVert_2$, which is axiom (N2). [step 1.5, L3, L4, L5]

3.1 By step 2.1 the middle term of step 1.3 satisfies $2\langle x,y\rangle \le 2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$, so $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} \le \lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2 + \lVert y\rVert_2^{2} = \bigl(\lVert x\rVert_2 + \lVert y\rVert_2\bigr)^{2}$. [step 1.3, step 2.1, L5, algebra]

4.1 Both $\lVert x+y\rVert_2$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 + \lVert y\rVert_2$ are nonnegative, so step 3.1 and monotonicity of squaring give $\lVert x+y\rVert_2 \le \lVert x\rVert_2 + \lVert y\rVert_2$, which is axiom (N3). [step 3.1, L3, L4]

5.1 Steps 2.4, 1.6 and 4.1 are exactly (N1), (N2) and (N3), so $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and for $n \ge 1$ the metric it induces is $d_2$; this is clause 2, and with steps 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 all four clauses are proved. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 1.6, step 4.1, L6] ∎

## Remarks

- **Which route to the triangle inequality was taken.** The proof above obtains (N3) by expanding $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}$ and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. The alternative is to quote [[thm-minkowski-finite]] at the rational exponent $p = 2$, which states the same inequality directly; that route is equally legitimate and is the one [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]] uses for a general exponent. Only one of the two is used here, so no statement is proved twice.

- **Clause 1 holds at $n = 0$, where it reads $0 \le 0$**, and the equality case is then satisfied by every pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$, the condition quantifying over no indices. Clause 2 also holds at $n = 0$, the zero space carrying exactly one norm ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). What is not available at $n = 0$ is the metric $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which is why the last sentence of clause 2 carries $n \ge 1$.

- **Clauses 3 and 4 are what the companion page uses.** The parallelogram law is an identity satisfied by every norm of the form $\sqrt{\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}$, so a norm violating it is not of that form; that is how the companion page rules out $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. Polarisation says the inner product carries no information the norm does not.

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integrable random variables $X,Y$.

[L1] Expectation is the Lebesgue integral against the probability measure ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

[L2] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$, the nonnegative integral is monotone, and the modulus of an integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[L3] Almost-everywhere equal integrable functions have equal integrals on every measurable event. ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])

[L4] The positive part of a measurable real function is measurable. ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Rewriting expectation as the integral by [L1], linearity in [L2] gives $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$ [L1, L2]

1.2 Applying the integral triangle inequality from [L2] after [L1] gives $$|\mathbb E[X]|=\left|\int X\,d\mathbb P\right|\le\int |X|\,d\mathbb P=\mathbb E[|X|].$$ [L1, L2]

2.1 If $X\le Y$ almost surely, put $D=Y-X$, which is integrable by [L2]. Its positive part $D^+=\max\{D,0\}$ is measurable by [L4] and integrable because $D^+\le|D|$. Since $D\ge0$ almost surely, $D^+=D$ almost surely, so [L3] gives $\int D\,d\mathbb P=\int D^+\,d\mathbb P\ge0$, where the last inequality concerns a pointwise nonnegative integrand. By [L1] and step 1.1, $0\le\mathbb E[Y-X]=\mathbb E[Y]-\mathbb E[X]$, so $\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y]$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L4]

3.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 prove the three assertions. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite product sigma-algebra convention, measurable coordinate maps, and the stated coordinate-permutation convention.

[F1] The finite product sigma-algebra is generated by the finite measurable rectangles. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F2] A measurable rectangle is a product of measurable sets in the coordinate spaces. [[def-measurable-rectangle]]

[F3] A map is measurable when the preimage of each measurable target set is measurable. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

[F4] A sigma-algebra is closed under complements and countable unions, hence under finite intersections. [[def-sigma-algebra]]

[A1] Each coordinate map $f_i$ is $\mathcal F/\Sigma_i$-measurable.

## Proof

1.1 By induction on $n$, the finite product sigma-algebra is generated by the $n$-coordinate rectangles. The base case is $n=1$. At the induction step, let $\mathcal S$ be the sigma-algebra generated by $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangles. For each measurable last-coordinate set $B$, the class of first-coordinate sets $A$ with $A\times B\in\mathcal S$ is a sigma-algebra: it contains the whole first product since the whole-first-product times $B$ is a coordinate rectangle, and complements and countable unions follow by relative difference inside that set and by countable unions. It contains the $n$-coordinate rectangles by construction, so it contains the recursively defined $n$-fold product sigma-algebra. Thus $\mathcal S$ contains every rectangle used in the recursive binary product. Conversely, each $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangle belongs to that recursive product sigma-algebra by its defining binary rectangle clause, so the two generated sigma-algebras agree. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 For a generating rectangle $E_1\times\cdots\times E_n$, its preimage under $f$ is $\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}(E_i)$. Each set in this finite intersection belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [A1], so the preimage belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [F4]. The class of target sets whose preimages under $f$ lie in $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra because preimages preserve complements and countable unions; by step 1.1 it contains the generators, so it contains the product sigma-algebra and [F3] makes $f$ measurable. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 For $\pi$ a permutation, $\tau_\pi^{-1}(E_1\times\cdots\times E_n)=E_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\times\cdots\times E_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$, which is a generating rectangle by [F2]. The same generated-sigma-algebra argument of step 2.1 proves that $\tau_\pi$ is measurable. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ and Borel-measurable functions $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$.

[L1] Measurability is equivalent to measurability of all strict upper (or lower) real threshold sets. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])

[L2] The parts are $h^+=\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\max(-h,0)$; $|h|=\max(h,-h)$. At every point one part is zero. ([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]])

[L3] Reflection reverses extended-real order. Partial addition excludes exactly the opposite-infinity pairs; addition with zero is defined. ([[def-extended-reals]])

[L4] The total function product $u\odot_X v$ is zero when either value is zero, is the real product on finite values, and otherwise is the infinity with the sign of the product. This includes all four ordered zero-infinity pairs. ([[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]])

[L5] A sigma-algebra contains $X$ and the empty set and is closed under finite intersections and countable unions; the rationals are countable, and between distinct real numbers lies a rational. ([[def-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-sigma-algebra-closure-laws]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]])

[L6] Finite real arithmetic is ordered-field arithmetic. ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Scalar multiples are measurable. If $c>0$, the product clauses give $\{cf>a\}=\{f>a/c\}$ for every real $a$, including infinite values of $f$. If $c<0$, they give $\{cf>a\}=\{f<a/c\}$. If $c=0$, $cf$ is constantly zero, whose threshold sets are $X$ or empty. Thus [L1] proves the claim, including measurability of $-f$. The latter agrees pointwise with reflection by the finite and the two infinite sign cases. [given, L1, L3, L4, L5, L6]

1.2 Assume $f+g$ is defined at every point. For every real $a$, $$\{f+g>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\bigl(\{f>q\}\cap\{g>a-q\}\bigr).$$ To check the right-to-left inclusion, both values then exceed finite bounds, hence neither is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$; otherwise finite ordered-field addition gives $f(x)+g(x)>a$. Conversely, a defined sum greater than $a$ cannot have a $-\infty$ summand. If both summands are finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<f(x)$. If $f(x)=+\infty$ and $g(x)$ is finite, choose $a-g(x)<q<a-g(x)+1$. If $g(x)=+\infty$ and $f(x)$ is finite, choose $f(x)-1<q<f(x)$. If both are $+\infty$, take $q=0$. These are all cases. The union is countable and each intersection is measurable, proving measurability of the sum. [L1, L3, L5, L6]

1.3 Let $u,v:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Their product is nonnegative by [L4], so its strict upper threshold set is $X$ when $a<0$. For real $a\ge0$, $$\{u\odot_X v>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}\bigl(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\}\bigr).$$ A point on the right has $u(x)>q>0$ and $v(x)>a/q\ge0$. If either value is infinite the product is $+\infty$; otherwise multiplying the strict finite bounds proves that the product exceeds $a$. Conversely, a product greater than $a\ge0$ has neither value zero. If both values are finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<u(x)$, which is possible because $u(x)v(x)>a$. If $u(x)$ is finite positive and $v(x)=+\infty$, choose $0<q<u(x)$. If $u(x)=+\infty$ and $v(x)$ is finite positive, choose $a/v(x)<q<a/v(x)+1$; this ensures $q>0$, also at $a=0$. If both values are $+\infty$, take $q=1$. These cases include $a=0$ and exclude zero-infinity pairs exactly because their product is zero. 2.1 For real $a$, total order gives $$\{\max(f,g)>a\}=\{f>a\}\cup\{g>a\},\qquad \{\min(f,g)>a\}=\{f>a\}\cap\{g>a\}.$$ The threshold criterion gives measurability. The zero function is measurable, so this also gives measurability of $f^+$, $f^-$ and $|f|=\max(f,-f)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L5]

[step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, L2, L3, L4]

4.1 The sum $h_++(-h_-)$ is therefore defined at every point. It is measurable by steps 1.1 and 1.2. It equals $f\odot_X g$: in the zero case both sides are zero; in the two same-sign cases step 3.1 leaves the nonnegative magnitude product in $h_+$ and zero in $h_-$, and in the two opposite-sign cases it leaves zero in $h_+$ and that magnitude product in $h_-$. ## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and measurable functions $f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

[L1] Threshold measurability characterizes extended-real measurability. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])

[L2] For each $x$, the limsup and liminf of the sequence $(f_n(x))$ satisfy

$$\limsup_n f_n(x) = \inf_n \sup_{k \ge n} f_k(x),\qquad \liminf_n f_n(x) = \sup_n \inf_{k \ge n} f_k(x),$$

and the pointwise limit exists exactly when the limsup and liminf are equal. ([[def-limsup-liminf]], [[thm-convergence-iff-limsup-equals-liminf]])

## Proof


**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $s(x):=\sup_n f_n(x)$ and $i(x):=\inf_n f_n(x)$. Then for every real [L1, given] $a$, $$\{s>a\} = \bigcup_n \{f_n>a\},\qquad \{i>a\} = \bigcup_{q \in \mathbb{Q},\, q>a}\ \bigcap_n \{f_n>q\}.$$ Since each threshold set on the right is measurable, [L1] gives measurability of $s$ and $i$. [L1, given]

2.1 For each $n$, the tail functions [step 1.1, L2] $s_n(x):=\sup_{k \ge n} f_k(x)$ and $i_n(x):=\inf_{k \ge n} f_k(x)$ are measurable by step 1.1. Applying step 1.1 again to the sequences $(s_n)$ and $(i_n)$ and then using [L2] yields measurability of $\limsup_n f_n$ and $\liminf_n f_n$. [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 Let $u:=\limsup_n f_n$ and $v:=\liminf_n f_n$. The equality set [step 2.1, L1, L2] $\{u=v\}$ is measurable because $$\{u=v\} = \bigcap_{q \in \mathbb{Q}} \Big(\big(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>q\}\big)\cup\big(\{u\le q\}\cap\{v\le q\}\big)\Big).$$ If $u(x)<v(x)$ or $v(x)<u(x)$, a rational strictly between them separates the two sides; if $u(x)=v(x)$, every rational lies on the same side of both values. So [L2] makes the pointwise-convergence set measurable. [step 2.1, L1, L2]

4.1 If $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then [L2] gives [step 2.1, step 3.1, L2] $f = \limsup_n f_n = \liminf_n f_n$. Since step 2.1 has already proved that both limiting functions are measurable, $f$ is measurable. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Gradients of scalar functions are Euclidean column vectors, with $Dg(\theta)[v]=\langle\nabla g(\theta),v\rangle$ under [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; vector expectations are taken coordinatewise.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$, and choose an open ball $U$ with $\theta_0\in U\subseteq\Theta$. Let $d,m\ge1$, let $N\ge0$ be a finite integer, let the states lie in $\mathbb R^m$, and let $\xi=(\xi_0,\ldots,\xi_N)$ collect fixed simulation inputs on one probability space. The maps are $u_0:\Theta\times E_0\to\mathbb R^m$, $\Psi_k:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\times E_{k+1}\to\mathbb R^m$, $\ell_k:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, and $\phi:\mathbb R^m\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$. Gradients of scalar functions are columns; $D_u\Psi_k$ is an $m\times m$ Jacobian and $D_\theta\Psi_k$ is an $m\times d$ Jacobian. Let
$u_0=u_0(\theta,\xi_0),\qquad u_{k+1}=\Psi_k(u_k,\theta,\xi_{k+1})\quad(0\le k<N).$
Assume the displayed step data maps are jointly measurable in all their arguments and, outside one probability-zero set, are continuously differentiable in their state and parameter variables on $U$. Define
$F_N(\theta,\xi):=\phi(u_N,\theta)+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\ell_k(u_k,\theta),\qquad J_N(\theta):=\mathbb E[F_N(\theta,\xi)].$
Assume $F_N(\theta,\xi)$ is integrable for every $\theta\in U$, and that there is a nonnegative integrable random variable $M$ with $\|\nabla_\theta F_N(\theta,\xi)\|_2\le M$ for all $\theta\in U$ almost surely, while $\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta F_N(\theta_0,\xi)\|_2^2<\infty$. Put $S_0=D_\theta u_0$, propagate
$S_{k+1}=D_u\Psi_k\,S_k+D_\theta\Psi_k,$
and define reverse variables by
$p_N=\nabla_u\phi(u_N,\theta),\qquad p_k=\nabla_u\ell_k(u_k,\theta)+(D_u\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1}.$
Then the discrete adjoint integrand
$\Gamma_N=\nabla_\theta\phi+S_0^\mathsf T p_0+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\nabla_\theta\ell_k+(D_\theta\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1}\right)$
satisfies $\nabla J_N(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma_N(\theta_0,\xi)]$.

For a family of discretizations indexed by $h$, if each discrete objective satisfies the preceding pathwise interchange hypotheses, $\mathbb E\|\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)\|_2\to0$, and the continuous-limit objective has derivative $\nabla J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma(\theta_0)]$ under the same pathwise interchange conditions, then $\nabla J_h(\theta_0)\to\nabla J(\theta_0)$. This conclusion gives no rate unless a quantitative bound on $\mathbb E\|\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)\|_2$ is also supplied. Euler–Maruyama is the special case $\Psi_k(u,\theta,\Delta W_k)=u+b(u,\theta)h_k+\sigma(u,\theta)\Delta W_k$, with $\Delta W_k$ the simulated Brownian increment.

All tangent, reverse and adjoint derivatives are evaluated on the common full-probability event where the sample maps are $C^1$. Define $\Gamma_N=0$ on its measurable null complement, and use this version in expectations.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite simulation graph, its differentiability and pathwise envelope hypotheses, and, for the final convergence assertion, $L^1$ convergence of the discrete adjoint integrands and the stated derivative representation of the continuous-limit objective.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of compositions of differentiable Euclidean maps are obtained by composing their total derivatives.

[F2] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at the initial index and inherited at each successor holds at every finite index.

[F3] [[thm-pathwise-simulation-gradient-is-unbiased-under-envelope]]: an integrable common envelope for a continuous pathwise gradient allows differentiation of its expected objective, with derivative equal to the expected pathwise derivative.

[F4] [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: each $\xi_k$ is a measurable random element. A constant parameter map is measurable because each measurable-set preimage is either empty or the whole probability space.

[F5] [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]: for a finite deterministic $C^1$ state-step graph, the tangent and reverse recursions in the Statement give its exact objective gradient.

[F6] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: the composite of two measurable maps is measurable once the inner map is measurable into the outer map's measurable domain.

[F7] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, and $\|z\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\langle v,z\rangle$ (equality is attained by $v=z/\|z\|_2$ when $z\ne0$).

[F8] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: expectation is linear for integrable scalar random variables.

[F9] [[lem-coordinate-maps-and-permutations-are-measurable-on-finite-products]]: a finite tuple of measurable coordinate maps is measurable into the finite product sigma-algebra.

[F10] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: finite sums, differences, real scalar multiples and products of finite real measurable functions are measurable.

[F11] [[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]: a pointwise limit of a sequence of measurable functions is measurable.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $\vartheta\in U$. By [F4] the constant map $\omega\mapsto\vartheta$ and each $\xi_k$ are measurable. The finite-tuple lemma [F9] first makes $\omega\mapsto(\vartheta,\xi_0(\omega))$ measurable; joint measurability of the initial-state map and composition [F6] then make $u_0(\vartheta,\xi_0)$ measurable. If $u_k$ is measurable, [F9] makes $\omega\mapsto(u_k(\omega),\vartheta,\xi_{k+1}(\omega))$ measurable into the step map's finite product domain, and [F6] makes $u_{k+1}$ measurable. Finite induction [F2] gives every state. Applying [F9] and [F6] to $(u_k,\vartheta)$ in each payoff map and then [F10] to the finite sum proves measurability of $F_N(\vartheta,\xi)$, also when $N=0$. Let $A$ be the common measurable null set excluded in the Statement. Fix a coordinate $j$ and put $h_n=1/(n+1)$ for $n\ge0$. If $\vartheta+h_ne_j\in U$, form the measurable difference quotient $Q_{j,n}=(F_N(\vartheta+h_ne_j,\xi)-F_N(\vartheta,\xi))/h_n$; otherwise put $Q_{j,n}=0$. Measurability follows from the fixed-parameter argument and [F10]. Replace each $Q_{j,n}$ by zero on $A$: equivalently multiply it by the measurable indicator of $A^c$, which remains measurable by [F10]. Since $U$ is open, these modified quotients converge at every outcome to the version of $\partial_jF_N(\vartheta,\xi)$ given by its derivative on $A^c$ and zero on $A$. By [F11] that version is measurable. This works for every fixed $\vartheta\in U$ and every coordinate, as required by [F3], without assuming the probability space is complete. The initial state is differentiable with sensitivity $S_0=D_\theta u_0$. If $u_k$ is differentiable, [F1] applied to $u_{k+1}=\Psi_k(u_k,\theta_0,\xi_{k+1})$ gives $D_\theta u_{k+1}=D_u\Psi_k\,D_\theta u_k+D_\theta\Psi_k$. Thus the stated tangent recursion holds for every $k<N$ by [F2]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F9, F10, F11]

2.1 Applying the chain rule to $F_N$ at $\theta_0$ gives its pathwise gradient $\nabla_\theta F_N=\nabla_\theta\phi+S_N^\mathsf T p_N+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\nabla_\theta\ell_k+S_k^\mathsf T\nabla_u\ell_k\right),$ where $p_N=\nabla_u\phi$. [given, F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix an input realization $\xi$ outside the common null set and set $x_0^\xi(\theta)=u_0(\theta,\xi_0)$, $\Psi_k^\xi(u,\theta)=\Psi_k(u,\theta,\xi_{k+1})$, $\ell_k^\xi(u,\theta)=\ell_k(u,\theta)$, and $\phi^\xi(u,\theta)=\phi(u,\theta)$. For $N\ge1$ this is a finite deterministic $C^1$ state-step graph on $U$, so [F5] applies. For $N=0$, $p_0=p_N=\nabla_u\phi$ and step 2.1 directly gives the derivative $\nabla_\theta\phi+S_0^Tp_0=\Gamma_0$. For each $k<N$, the definitions of $p_k$ and $S_{k+1}$ imply $S_k^\mathsf T p_k=S_k^\mathsf T\nabla_u\ell_k+S_{k+1}^\mathsf T p_{k+1}-(D_\theta\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1}.$ Rearrange and sum these identities over $k$: the $S_k^\mathsf T p_k$ terms telescope, and $p_N=\nabla_u\phi$. Thus $S_N^\mathsf T p_N+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}S_k^\mathsf T\nabla_u\ell_k =S_0^\mathsf T p_0+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\Psi_k)^\mathsf T p_{k+1},$ so the gradient in step 2.1 is exactly $\Gamma_N$, agreeing with [F5] when $N\ge1$. [given, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The pathwise derivative at $\theta_0$ is $\Gamma_N(\theta_0,\xi)$ by step 3.1. The Statement supplies integrability of $F_N$, the common integrable derivative envelope on $U$, and square-integrability at $\theta_0$. Thus [F3] gives $\nabla J_N(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma_N(\theta_0,\xi)]$. [given, F3, step 3.1]

5.1 In the discretization family, step 4.1 gives $\nabla J_h(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\Gamma_h(\theta_0)]$. For any integrable vector $Z$, [F7] and [F8] give, for every $\|v\|_2\le1$,
$\langle v,\mathbb EZ\rangle=\mathbb E\langle v,Z\rangle\le\mathbb E\|Z\|_2.$
Taking the supremum over such $v$ and using [F7] yields $\|\mathbb EZ\|_2\le\mathbb E\|Z\|_2$. Applying this to $Z=\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)$ yields $\|\nabla J_h(\theta_0)-\nabla J(\theta_0)\|_2=\|\mathbb E[\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)]\|_2\le\mathbb E\|\Gamma_h(\theta_0)-\Gamma(\theta_0)\|_2\longrightarrow0$ by the assumed $L^1$ convergence. ## Statement

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The total first-order expansions of $f$ at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$.

[L1] In the total-derivative definition, the normalized remainder tends to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r_f(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)=g(f(a))+Dg(f(a))k+r_g(k)$, with both normalized remainders tending to zero. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], $k=f(a+h)-f(a)=O(\|h\|_2)$; boundedness of $Dg(f(a))$ and the two remainder limits show both $Dg(f(a))r_f(h)$ and $r_g(k)$ are $o(\|h\|_2)$, including the case $k=0$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Substitution into the two expansions leaves $g(f(a+h))-g(f(a))-Dg(f(a))Df(a)h=o(\|h\|_2)$, and the composite of linear maps is linear. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathbb{N} = \omega$ is the smallest inductive set ([[def-inductive-set]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]); $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$.

[L1] $\omega$ is contained in every inductive set ([[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $0 = \varnothing \in S$ and ($x \in S \Rightarrow \sigma(x) = x \cup \{x\} \in S$). [given]

2.1 Then $S$ contains $\varnothing$ and is closed under $x \mapsto x \cup \{x\}$, so $S$ is an inductive set. [step 1.1]

3.1 $\mathbb{N} = \omega \subseteq S$ because $\omega$ is a subset of every inductive set. [L1, step 2.1]

4.1 With $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ by hypothesis, $S = \mathbb{N}$. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 The property form is the set case with $S = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : P(n)\}$: $P(0)$ and $P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$ give $0 \in S$ and $\sigma$-closure, so $S = \mathbb{N}$, i.e. $P$ holds for all $n$; conversely the set form is the property form applied to $P(n) :\equiv n \in S$, so the two are equivalent. [step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Gradients are Euclidean column vectors, and vector expectations are taken coordinatewise.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $H:\Theta\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the simulation payoff from [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]], and fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Suppose there is an open ball $U$ about $\theta_0$ such that for almost every $\omega$, $H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuously differentiable on $U$ and $\nabla_\theta H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuous there, and $\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\cdot)$ is measurable for every $\theta\in U$. Assume $\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega)\|_2\le M(\omega)$ for all $\theta\in U$ outside one measurable null set, where $M$ is nonnegative and integrable, and assume $\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)\|_2^2<\infty$. Then $J(\theta)=\mathbb E H(\theta,\cdot)$ is Fréchet differentiable at $\theta_0$ and
$\nabla J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)].$
Thus the pathwise estimator from [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]] is unbiased at $\theta_0$ and has finite coordinate variances.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The payoff and objective, $\theta_0$, the neighborhood and pathwise differentiability, the common integrable derivative envelope, and the square-integrable pathwise gradient in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]]: when the same random input is held fixed, the pathwise estimator is $D_\theta H(\theta,Z)$; the definition by itself does not assert unbiasedness.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for a differentiable composition, $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. Gradients are column vectors represented using the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], so $D_\theta H(\theta,\omega)[h]=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega),h\rangle$.

[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: if $q'$ is continuous on a compact interval, it is integrable there and $\int_a^b q'(t)\,dt=q(b)-q(a)$.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and [[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]]: for square-integrable $X$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb E X)^2\le\mathbb E[X^2]$.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $h\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\theta_0+h\in U$. For almost every $\omega$, set $q_\omega(t)=H(\theta_0+th,\omega)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F2], $q_\omega'(t)=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega),h\rangle$, which is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. The FTC [F3] gives
$H(\theta_0+h,\omega)-H(\theta_0,\omega)-\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle=\int_0^1\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle\,dt.$ [given, F2, F3]

1.2 For each such $h$, the random variable $M_h(\omega):=\sup_{r\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+rh,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega)\|_2$ is measurable: continuity in $t$ makes this countable supremum equal the supremum over $[0,1]$. It satisfies $0\le M_h\le2M$ almost surely. As $h\to0$, continuity of the sample gradient at $\theta_0$ gives $M_h\to0$ almost surely. [given, F1]

2.1 Taking expectations in step 1.1 and using [F6] bounds the absolute first-order remainder divided by $\|h\|_2$ by $\mathbb E M_h$. Along every sequence $h_n\to0$, [F4] with majorant $2M$ gives $\mathbb E M_{h_n}\to0$. Hence $J(\theta_0+h)-J(\theta_0)-\langle\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)],h\rangle=o(\|h\|_2),$ which is the Fréchet derivative formula. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4, F6, algebra]

3.1 Each coordinate of the unbiased estimator is square-integrable by the stated second-moment assumption. [F5] therefore gives finite variance for each coordinate. [given, F1, F5, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

## Statement

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open finite state-step graph, its $C^1$ maps, objective, trajectory and parameter in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]: $x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$ and $J=\phi(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n<N}\ell_n(x_n,\theta)$ with all displayed maps $C^1$.

[F2] [[alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiation]]: reverse mode accumulates each primitive pullback $D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$ at every parent slot in reverse topological order.

[F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: reverse mode returns the exact gradient of the finite $C^1$ real-arithmetic graph.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition. [F1, F4]

1.2 Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
